fishdesc.riverfishing.arapaima: Air is not optional here: the swim bladder works as a lung, and every ten or fifteen minutes the fish rolls up to gulp with a noise like a cork leaving a bottle. Three metres of armoured body, the rear scales edged in deep red, and a tongue of bone once used as a rasp. Males guard the fry in their mouths through the flood.
fishdesc.riverfishing.beluga: The heaviest freshwater fish there is: a sturgeon with a wide crescent mouth, a short blunt snout and flattened barbels, running to five metres and the better part of a tonne. It comes in from the sea and climbs the big rivers to spawn in spring and again in autumn, hunting herring and other fish along the bottom as it goes. Fish past a hundred years old have been recorded.
fishdesc.riverfishing.piraiba: The giant of Amazon catfish: a slab-sided grey body going on for nearly three metres, small eyes, and long trailing barbels that read the current for anything alive. It holds in deep channels and river holes, working at dusk and through the night, and swallows fish whole. Some populations run thousands of kilometres between the estuary and the headwaters, one of the longest migrations of any freshwater fish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.goliath_grouper: Built like a barrel, with a mouth as wide as its head and eyes that look too small for the animal, mottled brown and olive under dark spots. It holds station over wrecks, ledges and mangrove roots in warm shallows, inhaling crabs and fish in one gulp rather than chasing them. Intruders get a low boom drummed from its swim bladder, felt more than heard.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bull_shark: Short, thick and heavy through the shoulders, with a snout so blunt the profile looks squared off. The unusual part is internal: kidneys and a rectal gland that let it live in fresh water, which is why bull sharks turn up a thousand kilometres up the Mississippi and far into the Amazon. It hunts murky shallows, beaches and river mouths at first and last light, and gives ground to nothing.
fishdesc.riverfishing.frilled_shark: An eel-shaped shark from the cold deep: six frilled gill slits, the lowest pair meeting under the throat, and some three hundred needle teeth in backward-curving rows. What gets into that mouth does not come out. It hangs almost motionless above the bottom and strikes forward like a snake, mostly at squid. Gestation may run three and a half years, the longest of any vertebrate.
fishdesc.riverfishing.golden_dorado: Brass-gold flanks, red-edged fins and a black stripe running down the middle rays of the tail mark this South American characin. It runs the rapids and channels of big warm rivers and spills into flooded backwaters when the water rises. Heavy jaws and a blunt, muscular head let it batter through migrating shoals at dawn and dusk. Despite the gold and the name, its close relatives are piranhas.
fishdesc.riverfishing.golden_crucian: Bronze-gold and deep in the body, with a rounded back, a convex dorsal fin and, unlike the carp it gets mistaken for, no barbels at all. It thrives where other fish suffocate: stagnant ponds, swamps, overgrown ditches, even puddles that shrink through the summer. Buried in mud it survives frozen winters and months without oxygen. Where pike are about, it grows short and high-backed, awkward to swallow.
fishdesc.riverfishing.gorchak: No mussels, no bitterling: the female lays through a long tube into the gill chamber of a living freshwater mussel, and the young leave a month later. The fish is barely longer than a thumb, deep-bodied and half-transparent, with a blue-green stripe from mid-flank to the tail; spawning males turn pink and orange. Warm still ponds and river backwaters suit it, and it vanishes from sight after dark.
fishdesc.riverfishing.verkhovka: A finger-length fish with a bright silver stripe along the flank, an upturned mouth and a lateral line that gives up after five or six scales. Loose shoals sit at the surface of small ponds, ditches and flooded hollows, in water too shallow and stale for most other species. Females wind their eggs in spirals around plant stems and the male stands over them until they hatch.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sculpin: All head and pectoral fins, mottled brown to match gravel, and without a swim bladder, so it cannot hover - it props itself on the bottom and hops. Fast, cold, clean streams are a requirement, so its presence is a fair verdict on a river. It shelters under stones by day and creeps out at dusk after larvae and eggs. The male guards the clutch stuck to a stone's underside.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tubenose_goby: Barely a finger long, and named for the pair of short tubes, its front nostrils, that hang over the upper lip like a moustache. Pelvic fins fused into a suction disc let it sit on a stone without being washed off, which suits the shallow weedy margins of rivers, lagoons and brackish shores. The male takes a hollow under a stone, coaxes females in and guards the eggs alone.
fishdesc.riverfishing.kutum: A heavy Caspian relative of the roach, bright-scaled and broad across the shoulders, with a blunt head and thick lips built for crushing shells. Most of the year it stays in the brackish water along the coast, then pushes into the rivers in spring, which is when it appears in numbers. Feeding is bottom work: molluscs, worms, weed. Villages on the southern Caspian time whole celebrations to its arrival.
fishdesc.riverfishing.naked_carp: A domesticated carp bred without scales: bare, leathery skin over the whole flank, at most a stray plate near the tail. Still lakes and ponds suit it, where it grubs along the bottom for midge larvae, snails, seeds and soft shoots. Warm water sets it feeding hard, while cold shuts it down almost entirely. The naked skin marks easily, so an old fish carries a whole map of scars.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mullet: Warm coasts, harbours and river mouths hold shoals of this silver, cigar-shaped fish, its eye half-veiled by a fatty lid and its flank marked with faint grey stripes. It grazes algae and sediment near the surface and grinds the lot in a muscular, gizzard-like stomach. Autumn takes the shoals out to sea to spawn. A startled school comes clear of the water, fish after fish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.anglerfish: Two-thirds of it is head, and most of the head is mouth, set with teeth that curve inward; the rest tapers away as if added out of politeness. It lies half-buried in cold Atlantic mud, coloured exactly like the bottom, waving the fleshy tip of its first dorsal spine over the open jaws. The strike takes a few milliseconds, less than most prey needs to react.
fishdesc.riverfishing.black_marlin: Its pectoral fins give it away: rigid, unable to fold flat against the body, held out like stubby wings on any grown fish. The bill is short and heavy, the back slate-blue over a silver flank, and the biggest females pass seven hundred kilos. It hunts tuna and squid in the warm surface layers, and at speed it comes half out of the water in long flat leaps.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blobfish: Down where it belongs this is an ordinary-looking deep-sea sculpin; the famous melted face appears only at the surface, when gelatinous flesh lighter than water loses the pressure holding its shape. With almost no muscle and no swim bladder, it saves energy by lying on the bottom and swallowing whatever crustacean or mollusc drifts within reach. Day and night make no difference that deep.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluefin_tuna: A body machined into a spindle, the fins folding into grooves so that nothing breaks its profile, dark blue above and silver below. It is one of the few warm-blooded fish: heat exchangers in the muscle hold it several degrees above the sea, which lets it hunt cold water and cross the Atlantic in under two months. Pressed, it drives straight down rather than jumping, sounding hundreds of metres.
fishdesc.riverfishing.loach: By day it lies buried in the silt of swamps, ditches and weedy ponds; at dusk it comes out to root for worms and larvae. The body is eel-like, with a broad brown stripe along each flank and ten barbels around the mouth. It gulps air and breathes through its gut, so it outlives water that would kill anything else. Falling pressure makes it restless - hence the name weatherfish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.whale_shark: Twelve metres of spotted grey with a mouth a metre and a half wide and no teeth worth mentioning: the largest fish alive strains plankton, eggs and small shoaling fish through its gill rakers. The spot pattern over the back is unique to each animal and holds for life, which is how individuals are told apart. It cruises warm surface water by day and simply does not stop.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nelma: A whitefish that turned predator: silver-sided, big-scaled, with a jutting lower jaw and a mouth wide enough for a good smelt. Northern rivers and cold lakes hold it, and some fish drop into the brackish water of river mouths before turning back upstream. The run peaks in autumn, when spawning pulls it hundreds of kilometres against the current. Its relatives strain plankton; this one hunts fish all its life.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ocean_sunfish: A fish that seems to stop halfway: no real tail, only a ruffled flap where one should be, a grey disc of a body, two long fins beating up and down. The heaviest bony fish in the sea reaches a tonne on jellyfish and salps. Bright days it lies on its side at the surface, warming after deep dives while seabirds pick parasites off its skin.
fishdesc.riverfishing.pollock: Slim for a cod, olive-mottled, with a large eye suited to dim water and a lower jaw that runs slightly long. Enormous schools hang in midwater over the cold shelves of the North Pacific, rising and sinking with the plankton their prey follows. Winter draws them into the Bering Sea to spawn in the densest concentrations of fish anywhere. Most of the world's surimi and fish fingers begin here.
fishdesc.riverfishing.red_piranha: Deep and blunt-headed, silver flecked with gold, with a throat and belly the colour of fresh blood. The triangular teeth interlock like shears and are replaced through life, a whole quarter of the jaw at a time. It shoals through Amazon rivers and flooded forest in daylight, and the shoal is defence against otters and caimans as much as anything else. Most meals are fins, insects and carrion.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tiger_shark: Young fish carry the dark vertical bars that named the species; they fade with age until an old female looks plain grey. The teeth settle any doubt - short, deeply notched, serrated like a saw, shaped for cutting turtle shell. It patrols warm coasts and beach shallows at dusk and after dark, and its stomach contents are notorious: seabirds, rays, tin cans, licence plates.
fishdesc.riverfishing.linear_carp: One tidy row of big scales runs along the lateral line and the rest of the flank is bare, which is the point of the strain. The body is deep, the back thick, the barbelled mouth turned down for working soft ground in still, warm water. It roots through silt for midge larvae, snails and seeds at dawn, dusk and on into the night. Cold water simply switches it off.
legendary.riverfishing.halibut.credit: Dedicated to idkwho0457_07869 — for the Florida species and a long list of bugs found
fishdesc.riverfishing.peacock_bass: Not a bass at all but a big cichlid: olive-gold sides, three dark bars, and a gold-ringed black eyespot on the tail that gives the fish its name. Warm lagoons, oxbow lakes and slow tropical rivers suit it, while anything cool shuts it down. It hunts by sight in daylight and rests at night. Both parents shepherd the fry for weeks.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bullseye_snakehead: The name comes from the black, orange-rimmed spot at the base of the tail; the head above is flat and plated like a snake's. It lives in warm lowland lakes and swamps of southern Asia and gulps air at the surface, so it survives water that would suffocate most fish. Parents hover under a red cloud of fry and drive off anything that comes near.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mayan_cichlid: A black ocellus ringed in gold sits at the root of the tail, and six or seven dark bars cross flanks that flush deep red at the throat before spawning. It works mid-water in warm lowland lakes, backwater ponds and sluggish creeks from Mexico to Nicaragua, picking off insect larvae, snails and small crustaceans. Pairs guard their fry with real conviction. Cold shuts the species down completely.
fishdesc.riverfishing.oscar: A heavy, slab-sided cichlid in smoky brown and orange marbling, with a black spot ringed in orange at the base of the tail, a false eye that sends a piranha's bite to the wrong end. Slow backwaters, flooded forest and warm lakes of the Amazon basin are its ground, where it drifts, then inhales a small fish in one gulp. A pair cleans a stone and guards the eggs together.
fishdesc.riverfishing.striped_bass: Seven or eight dark stripes run level along the silver side, sharp enough to count in the water. The fish shuttles between surf beaches, estuaries and the rivers of eastern North America, running far upstream each spring to spawn. Its strongest seasons are spring and autumn, and it works dawn, dusk and darkness. The eggs drift with the current and must stay off the bottom to hatch.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluefish: Blue-green above and silver below, built like a hatchet, with jaws full of triangular teeth that meet like shears. Packs roam temperate and warm coasts on four continents, following shoals of small fish into the surf. When they corner one the water turns to foam, and they keep killing long after they are full. Autumn runs are the heaviest; cold water sends them away.
fishdesc.riverfishing.jack_crevalle: Blunt, steep-fronted head, a body compressed like a plate, and two dark marks to name it by: one on the gill cover, one at the base of the pectoral fin. Hard scutes armour the narrow wrist of the tail. Schools sweep warm beaches and reef edges, pushing far up rivers and into brackish creeks after prey and driving it against the surface. Pressure only makes it dig in harder.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tarpon: Scales the size of a coaster, a jutting lower jaw and a last dorsal ray drawn out like a whip make the silver king unmistakable. Warm coasts, beaches and river mouths hold it, and it pushes into brackish swamp water that would suffocate most fish. Its swim bladder doubles as a lung, so it rolls up to gulp air. Once moving it greyhounds, throwing its whole body clear.
fishdesc.riverfishing.snook: One unbroken black stripe runs the length of the silver flank, and the sloping head with its jutting lower jaw finishes the portrait. Mangrove roots, surf beaches and brackish river mouths hold them through the warm months, and a hard cold snap kills them outright. Hunting comes at first and last light and on into the dark. Most are born male and later become female.

guide.riverfishing.waiting.title: The wait: float & bottom
guide.riverfishing.waiting.text:
A float or bottom rod is NOT retrieved. Cast once, then leave it alone and watch.
• Any RMB while you wait REELS IT IN - it is not a slow retrieve. That one habit ruins the whole cast.
• No bite sound, no "Bite!" text. The float plunging or the rod tip twitching is the entire cue.
• RMB only once a fish has taken - that is the hookset.
• A bottom rod can sit on a rod pod and wait for you.
Only a lure rod is worked with clicks - see "Working the lure".
guide.riverfishing.drag.title: The drag
guide.riverfishing.drag.text:
Three drag states during a fight:
• Reeling (RMB) - locked: you reel in, tension rises.
• Idle - working: tension bleeds off slowly.
• Sneaking - OPEN: the spool slips. Tension drops 3× faster and the line cannot snap - but clicks gain NOTHING, and the spool pays out line the entire time it is open (1.5× faster during a run).
Open the drag during jumps and runs you cannot hold. You can only reel in while standing.
Tension bleed caps at 5 kg of drag; the effective strength it adds to the line continues scaling with the reel.
guide.riverfishing.stress.title: Tackle stress
guide.riverfishing.stress.text:
Overload no longer snaps the line instantly: past the limit, every tick rolls a break chance that scales with excess load and hold time.
Ease off and the tension drops. Surviving the strain still degrades line durability.
When the line actually snaps and takes the rig with it, the chat log shows the load in kg - though most over-pulls merely throw the hook. Match your tackle to the fish.
guide.riverfishing.livebait.title: Live bait
guide.riverfishing.livebait.text:
Fish under 150 g become live bait: use a crafting table - or hold the baitfish with a hook in the offhand, sneak, and right-click.
Live bait retains the fish's original weight: larger bait weeds out small fish and draws predators at least 4× its size.
A live-bait bottom rod can wait on a rod pod.
guide.riverfishing.groundbait.title: Groundbait 1: the base
guide.riverfishing.groundbait.text:
There is ONE groundbait: BASE GROUNDBAIT. Wheat seeds + bread makes two of it, and the fisherman sells it.

You can chum a spot with the base on its own and it works - it just isn't very effective. It sits dead center: neutral grind, neutral nutrition, no specific specialty. Everything after that is what you ADD to it.

## MAKING A MIX
• Put BASE GROUNDBAIT in a crafting grid together with UP TO 8 other ingredients. The base is required - corn and boilies on their own are not groundbait, they are additives.
• One SLOT is one item. A stack of 64 in a slot still counts as one, because the craft takes only one per slot.
• You get one groundbait out for every EDIBLE item in. Ballast - groundbait soil, clay - gives nothing back.
• A mix you made yourself is finished groundbait and cannot go back in the grid. Plain base can. That is what makes it the base.

## BALLAST IS THE IMPORTANT ONE
Soil and clay bring bulk, cloud, and color with zero calories, so they are how you make a mix leaner without making it worse.

## VANILLA IS A REAL SHELF
Wheat, bread, potatoes, and beetroots are early-game items, and over the base they mix into something that genuinely catches fish. You don't have to wait on a corn farm to start chumming.
guide.riverfishing.feeding.title: Groundbait 3: feeding
guide.riverfishing.feeding.text:
Right-click water to feed a 3x3 area. A baited spot cuts wait times by up to 40%% - about 1.5× more bites in the same timeframe. The center column applies full power; the outer ring counts at 60%%.

## YOU CANNOT OVERFEED
Throw as much as you like: more feed means more fish, and no spot ever suffers from extra chum. Maximum ATTRACTIVENESS is capped strictly by ingredients, never by quantity.

## IDENTICAL RECIPES STACK
A DIFFERENT RECIPE OVERWRITES THE SPOT - old bait doesn’t mix with new; it is erased immediately, and an alert will confirm the replacement. Balance your blend in the crafting grid, not by tossing several different mixes into the water. Adding dye does not make a recipe unique.

A feeder, flat feeder, carp method, or cage rig expels one charge per cast WHERE THE TACKLE LANDS - not at your feet. It creates the exact same baited spot as a right-click, so feeding by hand or by cage builds up the same swim.

## DURATION
Lasts 3 to 12 minutes based on fraction. Fine dust loses half its strength every 90 seconds and disperses quickly; whole grains halve every 4.5 minutes and remain on the bottom. That longevity sustains longer bottom-fishing sessions.

Fish present over the spot, but no bites? It is never about quantity. Check your grind, nutritional richness, or species menu.
guide.riverfishing.gbnumbers.title: Groundbait 2: the numbers
guide.riverfishing.gbnumbers.text:
Nutrition and fraction are the average over everything in the mix, weighted by quantity and including ballast. That is how ballast dilutes: it averages in zeros.

Four factors decide how well the baited spot works FOR A GIVEN SPECIES.

## FRACTION - the grind
A COARSE FRACTION CALLS BIG FISH: dust for bleak and roach, whole grain and boilies for bream and carp. This is the real answer to "why do I only catch tiddlers" - it is a choice, not a bug. Over a coarse carpet, the size roll also flattens, meaning the fish that arrive roll heavier - but only past a fraction of 0.50; a mix at the base's own grind flattens nothing. A better chance, never a guarantee.

## NUTRITION - how much food is down there, and how much this species wants
A carp wants a laid table; a bleak wants a cloud, and the table set for carp is not what it came for. This is why "just throw boilies" fails: boilies are the richest and coarsest feed available, making them ideal for carp and useless for roach.

## THE MENU - what is actually in it
If a fish eats worms, chopped worm in the mix works; its guide entry lists what it takes. The base and ballast are entirely neutral, which is why plain base is neither the right food nor the wrong food.

## VARIETY - and here is what people miss
TWO numbers dictate a spot:
• the SCORE, from the four factors above - WHO comes.
• the CAP, from nutrition and variety - HOW MANY come. Plain base maxes out at 0.48 of maximum attraction; the base plus four rich ingredients hits 0.94, and you cannot go higher in a 3x3 grid.
A mix of three can score a perfect 1.00 and still lose to a five-ingredient mix at 0.90, because the five-part spot holds more fish. Aim for the BASE PLUS THREE OR FOUR ingredients.

Feeding more reaches the cap faster. It never raises it.
guide.riverfishing.gbrecipes.title: Groundbait 4: recipes
guide.riverfishing.gbrecipes.text:
Ready-made recipes are a BASELINE, NOT A LIMIT. Each was tested against its target species - and each can be outperformed by fine-tuning it for your specific water.

Numbers indicate how many items go into the crafting grid. Every recipe starts with base groundbait, as required.

## HOUR ONE, no farm yet
  Base 3 + Wheat 2 + Bread 3 + Potato 1

## BLEAK, ROACH, RUFFE, GUDGEON - also winter and pressured water
  Base 1 + Maggot 1 + Bloodworm 1 + Wheat Seeds 3

## BREAM, white bream, blue bream, vimba, sabrefish
  Base 1 + Maggot 3 + Worm 1 + Wheat Seeds 2

## TENCH, crucian carp, ide
  Base 2 + Dough 2 + Maggot 2 + Corn 1

## CARP, mirror carp, wild carp
  Base 1 + Corn 3 + Boilie 3 + Pea 2

## GRASS CARP, silver carp
  Base 1 + Corn 3 + Pearl Barley 3 + Boilie 1

## CATFISH, eel, burbot
  Base 2 + Boilie 1 + Worm 3 + Chicken Liver 3

## STURGEON, channel catfish
  Base 1 + Boilie 1 + Worm 1 + Chicken Liver 3

## STERLET, nase - the plain worm swim
  Base 1 + Clay Ball 1 + Worm 3

## COD, flounder, conger, saithe
  Base 1 + Raw Fish Fillet 3 + Dried Kelp 1

The bream mix scores a perfect 1.00 across all five species because their grind preference, appetite, and bait lists match. The sterlet mix also hits 1.00 but holds a thin swim - it only has three ingredients, one of which is clay. Add a fourth edible ingredient when you need volume rather than a precision bite.
guide.riverfishing.community.title: Every water is its own
guide.riverfishing.community.text:
Each water body has its own population: some species simply DO NOT live here, while 1–3 are signature fish that bite almost twice as eagerly.
A small pond has few species; a large river or lake is rich. In big waters, fish hold in specific spots - look for productive drop-offs, holes, and banks.
Ubiquitous small fish (rotan, roach, perch, bleak) live everywhere - no water is ever truly barren.

## FAUNAL PROVINCES
Beyond weather, geography rules: the world is divided into four faunal provinces - regions roughly three thousand blocks across. A species native to one is ENTIRELY ABSENT from the others, not merely rare. Nothing done on the bank will put taimen and peacock bass in the same river: travel to the fish, or bring specimens home to breed them. The ocean is undivided.

## THE FISH FINDER
Three views on one display:
• The SECTION shows the bottom profile along your line of sight, plotting every fish at its current depth alongside a species list. Click an entry to see what the mod knows about it locally, including conditions preventing a bite.
• The CHART displays that same bed from above - blank until someone casts across it - and zooms out far enough to reveal provincial borders.
• The SAMPLE tracks environmental metrics: water clarity, climate, current seasonal third, dissolved oxygen, available cover, ecosystem health, and the local fishery ledger.

## STOCKING
Missing a target species? Stock the water - but treat it as selective breeding, not a simple roll of the dice. If the water cannot support the fish, stocking fails immediately; if only the continent is mismatched, the ledger will state so.
Otherwise, introduced fish enter the register, and the species PERMANENTLY SETTLES once breeding stock - a mature pair or thirty fry - survives an entire spawning window in water that meets at least half its requirements. Until then, introduced fish remain TEMPORARILY catchable from the stocked pool, dispersing entirely if breeding fails. A species settled outside its native biome thrives at only 25%% base strength - but survives.
Stock accumulates by biomass: a trophy counts as three standard fish, whereas fry contribute negligible weight. Native stocks scale up to 250%% bite activity, while introduced populations cap at 150%%; overstocked schools (>125%%) thin out 25%% faster.
Release your trophies: catch-and-release is what sustains the fishery.
guide.riverfishing.lurework.title: Working the lure
guide.riverfishing.lurework.text:
The retrieve is driven by RMB CLICKS: each click turns the spool once, drawing the lure toward the bank.
• Wobblers & crankbaits: work only on a STEADY rhythm (roughly one click every half-second). Break the cadence and the action dies - fish will follow, then turn away.
• Spinners, spoons, jigs, soft plastics: forgive nearly any retrieve speed - just keep them moving.
• Topwaters: click with DELIBERATE PAUSES - each pop after a pause draws strikes from below.
Holding RMB reels in too quickly: the line comes back, but bite rates plunge fivefold - fish rarely strike a rushing lure.
A lure left dead in the water never draws a strike.
guide.riverfishing.topwater.title: Topwater
guide.riverfishing.topwater.text:
Work the popper in a cadence: short crank - pause - crank again. Every pop after a pause calls the fish; continuous reeling drags it under.
A boil swells behind the lure before the strike, and the hit blows up the surface.
The hookset window is short - be ready.
guide.riverfishing.trolling.title: Trolling
guide.riverfishing.trolling.text:
An assembled trolling rod (or sea spinning rod) in hand + a boat + three seconds of steady speed - and line pays out automatically behind the stern.
Maintain your speed: too slow sinks the lure, too fast spooks the fish.
The lure trails behind the boat as long as you want - no need to reel it back in.
No hookset required either: the boat's momentum sets the hook automatically. Fish on - cut speed and fight it.
Pelagic species (mahi-mahi, wahoo, tuna, marlin) roam exclusively over deep open water.
guide.riverfishing.biggame.title: Sea giants
guide.riverfishing.biggame.text:
Tuna dive deep: during a run it STRIPS line - never force it; pump the rod back between runs.
Marlin and sailfish breach: never reel during a jump - loosen the drag and let it ride, or the hook tears out.
Toothy predators (shark, wahoo, barracuda) strictly require a steel or titanium leader.
guide.riverfishing.legendary.title: Legendary fish
guide.riverfishing.legendary.text:
Certain species hide a SINGLE named trophy per server - from the Queen of the Snags to the Megalodon.
The catch is broadcast server-wide and engraved into server history forever.
There will never be another.
guide.riverfishing.market.title: Market and the daily order
guide.riverfishing.market.text:
The fisherman's prices are dynamic: every prime fish sold on the server slightly saturates that species' market, eventually cutting payouts by up to half. Demand recovers at roughly 15%% per day - a two-week rebound, not an overnight reset - so overfish bream and that income dries up.
Each day features an ORDER OF THE DAY: that chosen species pays ×2.5, market glut be damned.

## THE CONTRACT BOARD
Beside his stall stands the contract board, and that is where the real money is. Each fisherman posts THREE jobs daily - one board per villager, so two fishermen mean two distinct boards - and those three tasks remain active all day for everyone, persisting through server restarts. Claim a task as a contract slip; you can hold two at a time.
The slip specifies not just the fish, but HOW to catch it: from a river, on a float rod, using worms, after dark. Only a fish landed under those exact criteria counts. The board displays the conditions as an active checklist verified against your current spot and equipped tackle - inspect one and you learn how to catch that fish. You have seven days to complete it.
Turn it in with the catch to receive emeralds, journal XP, and REPUTATION. At 5, 15, and 30 reputation points, a secret trading tier opens that the rest of the village never sees. Poaching drains that reputation right back down.

guide.riverfishing.spook.title: The fish notice you before they notice the bait
guide.riverfishing.spook.text:
Every fishing spot remembers a brief scare. It is NOT the long depletion of a swim - it lasts 30 to 90 seconds and then wears off.
What frightens the fish: running and jumping on the bank within ~6 blocks, standing IN the water, breaking a block nearby, a moving boat, your own shadow on the water when the sun is low behind you - and the cast itself, where the tackle lands.
While the fish are spooked, bites stop and visible fish scatter. Watch the water: the ripples spreading outward are your cue.
The only real answer is simple: walk up, sneak, and stay still. Crouched and motionless, you make no noise at all.
This is what a long cast is FOR: what you do on the bank cannot reach out there, and the only thing that spooks the fish at distance is the splash of your tackle landing.
Murky and deep water forgets you in half a minute; clear shallows and a small pond stay wary for a minute and a half.
guide.riverfishing.coop.title: Fishing together
guide.riverfishing.coop.text:
Everyone nearby sees the fight - the boss bar appears for spectators within 12 blocks.
A friend can NET your fish: empty hand, crouch right beside you when the fish is close to the bank.
It counts for both players - the helper earns journal XP.
guide.riverfishing.thanks.title: Thanks
guide.riverfishing.thanks.text:
This mod is built by one person, but almost nothing in it was conceived alone.
38raspberry and Gabbi helped directly with development - hands on the code and assets, not just advice from the sidelines. Much of what you fish with exists thanks to them.
And the features below exist because players specifically asked for them:
idkwho0457_07869 - the Florida nine, the entire Amazon roster (arapaima, piraiba, golden dorado), the bull shark, and the goliath grouper. Effectively a third of the mod's species.
Colin_Brittan - a commercial fisherman in real life: the frilled shark and beluga, sitting at tier 12 at the very peak of progression.
белебобик - the sculpin and tubenose goby, along with tracking down the biome bug behind them.
vptareo-aao - splitting crucian carp into Prussian (silver) and crucian (golden), plus the electrofisher: a dedicated way to clear nuisance fish from specific waters.
Dmitriy_Smile - expanding freshwater variety, especially the cyprinid (carp) family.
arsen_501 - making line, hook, and rig tiers a meaningful tactical choice rather than linear upgrades.
oneshot - prompting the formal clarification: ambient fish models are purely rendered client-side, not spawned entities, costing the server zero performance.
If someone is missing or something is stated wrong, let us know on Discord. That feedback is how every line above was made.

fishdesc.riverfishing.bream: A line of bubbles rising over a silty flat usually means a shoal below, standing nose-down and blowing bloodworm out of the mud. The fish itself is deep and slab-sided, heavy with slime, bronze in old specimens and bright silver in young ones, with a long anal fin and a mouth that telescopes downward. It runs hard once, then turns broadside and quits.
fishdesc.riverfishing.crucian_carp: Few fish put up with as much: a pond frozen almost to the bed, summer stagnation, a ditch drying down to a puddle. Bronze to slate-grey, deep in the body, with no barbels and a serrated spine at the front of the dorsal that separates it from a small common carp. It roots through soft bottom for larvae and detritus. Some populations are entirely female.
fishdesc.riverfishing.roach: Shoals hang in mid-water in nearly every river and lake from Ireland to Siberia, which makes this the default fish of half a continent. Silver flanks, a blunt snout and an orange-red iris separate it from a young rudd. It grazes weed, snails and whatever drifts past, mostly at first and last light, and keeps feeding through winter under the ice.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rudd: Blood-orange fins and a mouth angled sharply upward mark this one out, and the iris is golden-yellow where a roach's is red. It holds just under the surface of still, weedy lakes, backwaters and warm swamp margins, taking insects off the film and nipping soft plants. Summer is its season; by late autumn it has all but vanished. A kilo fish is a rarity.
fishdesc.riverfishing.white_bream: The eye is the tell: much bigger than a true bream's on a fish of the same length, set in a rounder, flatter body of cold silver. Orange washes the base of the pectoral and pelvic fins. Tight shoals shuffle over the bottom of slow rivers and lakes, sifting silt for larvae, snails and small crustaceans. A kilo is about its ceiling; most fit in one hand.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp: Heavy-shouldered and fully scaled in bronze, with thick rubbery lips and two pairs of barbels at the corners of the mouth. It vacuums the bottom of warm lakes and slow rivers, tipping head-down over silt and leaving a trail of bubbles. Spawning is a summer riot in flooded weed, loud enough to hear from the bank. Carp learn caution fast, live for decades, and have been carried nearly everywhere.
fishdesc.riverfishing.catfish: Two long barbels on the upper jaw, four short ones below, a broad flat head and a naked, slick body and an anal fin running nearly to the tail. Days pass in deep holes and sunken timber in warm rivers and lakes; at dusk it moves onto the shallows for fish, frogs and whatever fits. Heat wakes it, winter shuts it off completely. The biggest in Europe pass two metres.
fishdesc.riverfishing.perch: Dark bars down a green-gold flank, a black blotch at the rear of the spiny first dorsal and orange-red pelvic fins leave little room for doubt. Small ones hunt fry in packs along reeds and pilings, while the humpbacked old loners hold deeper and eat their own kind without ceremony. Autumn brings them together and feeding is hardest then. They strike in a short bullish rush and bore downward.
fishdesc.riverfishing.pike: Built as one long lever: a duck-billed snout full of backward-slanting teeth, and dorsal and anal fins set right at the back for a single explosive lunge. Olive flanks broken by pale bars dissolve into the weed beds of lakes and slow rivers. Autumn is its season, when it feeds heavily before the cold and thinks nothing of taking a pike two-thirds its own length.
fishdesc.riverfishing.zander: Glassy, light-gathering eyes are the whole point of the zander: a mirror layer behind the retina lets it hunt in murk and darkness while its prey is blind. The body is long and firm, the front dorsal fin spined, and four true fangs stand among the smaller teeth. It patrols hard bottoms and drop-offs in rivers and big lakes. A narrow throat limits it to slim fish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.gudgeon: Cigar-shaped and sand-coloured, marked with a line of dark blotches along the side and carrying one short barbel at each corner of the mouth. It rests on clean sand and gravel in running water, propped on its pectoral fins, darting a few inches at a time after larvae and worms. The shoals stay busy in daylight, even in cold water. Silt and pollution drive it out at once.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ruffe: Dusk is when it wakes: a small, humpbacked bottom-dweller that grubs through silt for bloodworm, larvae and the eggs of better-regarded fish long after the light has gone. Olive-brown flanks carry dark freckles, the dorsal runs as one spiny ridge, and the whole animal is coated in slime. Cold water suits it, so autumn and winter are its season. Both gill covers end in needle points.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bleak: A thin flash of silver no longer than a hand, with an upturned mouth for picking insects off the surface film. Bleak swarm in the top layer of rivers and lakes through the warm months and only in daylight, then vanish from sight once the water cools. Their scales come loose at a touch, and the pearly coating was once boiled down by the thousand for artificial pearls.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ide: Silver with a brassy cast, small-headed and thick through the shoulder, with rust-red fins below, the ide is often taken for a chub until the finer scales settle the argument. It travels mid-water in rivers, shy and quick to leave, feeding at first and last light and busiest in spring. A golden form, the orfe, is kept in ornamental ponds. Big ones bore deep and give no ground.
fishdesc.riverfishing.chub: Under overhanging branches, where something is always dropping into the water, the chub holds near the surface and takes whatever arrives: beetles, cherries, a frog, a careless mouse. Big scales rimmed in dark give the flank a netted look, and the lower fins are the colour of rust. Warm summer days suit it; cold water shuts it down. It fights in short, bullish runs.
fishdesc.riverfishing.asp: A carp-family fish that took up hunting: silvery, deep-shouldered, and without a single tooth in its jaws. It works the surface of big rivers in broad daylight and all but stops feeding once the water goes cold. The hunt is loud - it charges a shoal and slaps the water flat with its tail, then collects the stunned fish. Nothing else in a European river makes that noise.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tench: Thick slime coats the tench so heavily that its minute scales all but disappear, leaving a dark olive fish with small orange eyes and rounded fins. It works the mud of ponds, swamps and weedy lake margins, warm still water above all, and feeds hardest at first light. Winter shuts it down completely: it beds into the bottom and waits. Old country lore called it the doctor fish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.burbot: The only cod that never sees salt water: mottled yellow and brown, long in the tail, with one barbel under the chin. Summer heat drops it into a torpor beneath stones; it wakes as the water cools, feeding at night through autumn and hunting hardest under the ice. Spawning falls in the coldest weeks, in a slow writhing ball of fish on gravel. Its liver is enormous.
fishdesc.riverfishing.eel: Snake-bodied and slick, with a single fin skirting the tail and scales so small they seem absent. It lies buried in silt and roots by day and travels the bottom at night, feeding by scent in water too dark for eyes. Warm summers wake it, cold shuts it down entirely. Every mature eel eventually leaves fresh water for the Sargasso Sea, spawns once and dies.
fishdesc.riverfishing.grayling: A tall sail of a dorsal fin, marked with rows of dark spots and washed with violet, rides over a slim, small-mouthed body. Cold, clear, quick rivers of mountain and taiga country are its whole range, and it holds in mid-water behind stones, facing up into the flow for drifting insects. Feeding carries on through the cold months. Fresh from the river it smells faintly of thyme.
fishdesc.riverfishing.trout: Butter-gold flanks carrying black and rust-red spots, each in a pale halo, and a tail cut almost square. It keeps one lie behind a boulder or under a cut bank all season, letting the current bring food, and drives off smaller fish that try the same spot. Cold mountain and forest streams; autumn brings spawning on clean gravel. The biggest turn nocturnal and live almost entirely on other fish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sterlet: Smallest of the sturgeons and the easiest to name: a long narrow snout, fringed barbels beneath it, and more lateral bony scutes than any relative carries. Rivers only, with clean sand and gravel under a steady current, and the feeding is night work over the bottom for larvae, worms and small molluscs. Spring draws it upstream to spawn on shoals. By day it settles into deep holes and barely stirs.
fishdesc.riverfishing.wild_carp: The undomesticated original: fully scaled in bronze and gold, longer and leaner than any pond strain, with a long dorsal fin and a serrated leading spine. Rivers with current are its home, though big lakes suit it, and it feeds head-down over the bottom among roots and silt. Summer is its season; cold sends it dormant into deep holes. A life spent against the current shows in the shoulders.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mirror_carp: Bare, leathery skin broken by a few huge plate-like scales - sometimes a row along the lateral line, sometimes a random scatter, never the same pattern twice. It is a domesticated common carp, bred in monastery ponds so the fish would be easier to clean. Warm still water and soft bottoms suit it, and it roots through silt on summer evenings. A big one moves off in one unstoppable surge.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_kohaku: White as a plate, with red laid over it in bold islands and not a trace of black - the moment black appears the fish is something else entirely. Breeders judge the edge of the red: it should end sharply, as if cut. A bottom feeder in ponds and slow lakes, it grazes silt all day and keeps at it after dark.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_tancho_sa: One round red spot on the crown and no red anywhere else - that is the entire demand made of a Tancho, and why it borrows the name of the red-crowned crane. The rest is white with a scatter of black. Judging comes down to the spot: how round it sits, how squarely centred between the eyes. Peaceable, unhurried, always near the bottom.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_showa_san: Black is the ground colour here, not a decoration: it wraps right around the body and pushes up into the head, with red and white broken over the top. Wedges of black at the base of the pectoral fins mark a true Showa. Heavy and unhurried near the bottom, it feeds at any hour on larvae, snails and weed, and spawns among flooded grass.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_asagi: Blue-grey scales laid in a neat net across the back, with red running along the belly, the cheeks and the base of every fin. The oldest pattern still kept in Japanese ponds, and the evenness of that net decides what a fish is worth. Asagi work the floor of still water for larvae and soft weed, going dormant in the cold and spawning in spring shallows.
fishdesc.riverfishing.carp_koi_bekko: A clean single-colour body - white, red or yellow - carrying a scatter of black ink blots down the flanks, like the shell of a tortoise. The head must stay unmarked; one spot on the forehead and the fish drops a grade. These carp nose along the pond floor through the day and half the night, taking larvae, snails and whatever soft food the silt gives up.
fishdesc.riverfishing.grass_carp: Torpedo-shaped rather than deep-bodied, with a broad flat forehead, no barbels and large scales edged in dark. It is a vegetarian on an industrial scale, mowing pondweed and young reed in warm lakes and quiet river backwaters and eating close to its own weight in a good week. Real appetite arrives only in properly warm water; winter stops it dead. Native to the Amur, it now turns up almost everywhere.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluegill: Colonies of saucer-shaped nests fanned into the shallows are the work of the males, who defend them well past sense. The fish is round as a plate, olive with faint bars, a solid black flap on the gill cover and an orange breast on breeding males. It holds mid-water by weed beds and sunken timber in warm lakes and ponds, tipping up for insects and snails.
fishdesc.riverfishing.largemouth_bass: The jaw is the giveaway: it hinges back past the eye, wide enough to take prey nearly half the fish's own length. Olive-green with a broken dark band along the flank, the bass lies up in weed and drowned timber in warm lakes and ponds, ambushing at dawn and dusk. In spring the male fans a nest and guards the fry for weeks. Cold water switches it off.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rainbow_trout: A magenta band down the side and black speckling scattered over back, fins and tail identify it at a glance. Native to Pacific North America, it now runs wild in cold rivers from Patagonia to the Himalaya. A spring spawner, keenest at first light, it resists in short jumping bursts rather than long runs. The sea-going steelhead comes back twice the size.
fishdesc.riverfishing.channel_catfish: Slate-olive with a deeply forked tail and, in young fish, dark spots that fade with the years; the upper jaw overhangs the lower. American rivers and reservoirs are its home ground, though it has been spread far beyond them, holding on the bottom where current meets slack. It works at night, guided by taste buds spread over the entire skin. Males guard the eggs in a hollow until they hatch.
fishdesc.riverfishing.silver_carp: Eyes set low on the head, below the line of the mouth, and a sharp keel along the belly. Gill rakers fused into a fine sieve let it strain algae from mid-water, so it grazes the green soup of warm lakes and slow rivers, not the bottom. Summer heat is its feeding season; under ice it does almost nothing. Startled, a whole shoal launches clear of the surface at once.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sabrefish: Straight-backed, with the belly drawn out into a sharp keel and long wing-like pectorals, the sabrefish looks like a blade laid on its side. Shoals travel the open water of big rivers just under the surface, chasing fry and lifting insects off the top with an upturned mouth. Warm months and bright hours are its own. A kilo and a half is about the ceiling.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blue_bream: Slim, blue-backed and slab-sided, with a small upturned mouth and an anal fin so long it hangs like a fringe under the tail. Unusually for the family it feeds in open water rather than on the bottom, sieving plankton in the middle layers of rivers and reservoirs. The shoals move steadily, without fuss. Even an old fish rarely tops eight hundred grams.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mackerel: Wavy black bars over a blue-green back, a body tapering into a row of small finlets, a stiff crescent tail: everything about the mackerel serves speed. It carries no swim bladder, so it cannot stop, and the schools cover long distances after plankton and small fish through open temperate seas. Summer brings them close inshore. Few fish of two kilos pull as hard.
fishdesc.riverfishing.herring: Steel-blue over a mirror-bright body, with a sharply keeled belly and scales so loose they come away at a touch. Schools run through the cold North Atlantic in bands kilometres long, straining copepods and fish larvae from open water. Spawning stocks return to the same gravel banks generation after generation. No other fish has moved so much money or set so many countries arguing over a border.
fishdesc.riverfishing.garfish: Long and pencil-thin, the jaws drawn out into a beak full of small teeth, the back the colour of deep water. It runs at the surface of warm European seas through summer, chasing sprat and sandeel and skittering clear of the waves when pressed. The oddity is the skeleton: the bones are bright green from a harmless pigment, which puts a great many people off eating it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.seabass: Plain silver, deep-bodied, with a spiny first dorsal and gill covers sharp enough to open a careless hand. It hunts broken water along the European coast - surf beaches, harbour walls, estuary mouths - and works dusk and darkness through the warm months. Growth is slow, so a five-kilo fish has often lived two decades. Cold winters push the shoals off the beaches into deeper water.
fishdesc.riverfishing.flounder: Born symmetrical, it turns as a fry: one eye creeps over the skull until both sit on the right side, and the fish spends its life lying on its blind flank. Rough tubercles run along the lateral line and the fin bases, and the brown upper side shifts tone to match sand or silt. It works cold sea beds for worms and crustaceans, mostly after dark, and spawns in winter.
fishdesc.riverfishing.cod: A single barbel hangs from the chin, and the pale lateral line arcs over mottled olive-brown flanks. Cold North Atlantic shelves hold them near the bottom, deepest in winter, when they gather to spawn and a big female sheds millions of eggs. They feed hard, then sulk for days. Whole coastal economies stood on this fish, and the Grand Banks were emptied of it within a lifetime.
fishdesc.riverfishing.saithe: Dark green-black above, with a lateral line so straight and pale it looks ruled onto the flank, and a lower jaw that pushes past the upper. Shoals patrol the cold North Atlantic in midwater over reefs, wrecks and drop-offs, chasing herring and sandeel at speed. Young fish crowd harbours and shallows while the old ones go deep. Pound for pound it pulls harder than the cod beside it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.conger: Scaleless, grey-brown and in old females as thick through as a thigh, with a dorsal fin that begins just behind the pectorals. Days go by wedged into rock crevices and wreck timbers on the sea floor; it comes out at dusk and hunts all night. Once it has chosen a direction it pulls without pause, usually straight back toward its hole. Congers spawn once in deep water and then die.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ray: Flat, diamond-shaped and rough as sandpaper, with a row of stout curved thorns down the midline of back and tail. It lies half-buried on sand and gravel in coastal and offshore seas, quiet through the day, and works the bottom after dark for crabs, worms and small fish. A first hard rush gives way to dead weight, the flat body clamped against the ground. Eggs go into horned leathery cases.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mahi: Alive it is green-gold shot through with electric blue and dark speckling; out of the water the colour drains away in under a minute. Males grow a squared, almost vertical forehead that females never develop. It hangs at the surface of warm ocean around drifting weed and floating timber, chasing flying fish through the daylight. Growth is absurdly fast, and a fish can pass a metre inside its first year.
fishdesc.riverfishing.wahoo: Long as a fence rail and about as slim, steel-blue, with two dozen cobalt bars along the side that fade within minutes of the fish leaving the water. The snout is beak-like, the teeth triangular and razored. It crosses warm blue ocean alone or in loose handfuls rather than in true schools, feeding through the brighter hours. Everything about it serves one short, violent burst of speed.
fishdesc.riverfishing.yellowfin_tuna: Blue-black over the back with a gold band down the side, and in big fish the second dorsal and anal fins draw out into long yellow sickles. Schools roam warm, deep ocean at mid-depth, often travelling under pods of dolphins, and feed through daylight with a peak at dawn. Body heat above the surrounding water keeps the muscles working far down. Pressed hard, it sounds straight down and stays there.
fishdesc.riverfishing.barracuda: Long and cylindrical, silver-flanked, with a jutting lower jaw carrying teeth of two sizes: small ones to grip, daggers to cut. Adults show scattered dark blotches along the rear of the lower flank. It hangs motionless in warm reef and coastal water, apparently asleep, then covers several body lengths in a single burst. What usually brings it close to a diver is curiosity rather than hunger.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blue_marlin: Cobalt above, silver below, a row of pale blue bars along the flank that flare and fade with mood, and a dorsal drawn to a point instead of a rounded sail. Females reach four times the weight of males, so every very large blue marlin is one. Warm open water far from land is its ground, and at speed it leaves the surface in long leaps.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sailfish: The sail gives it away: a dorsal fin taller than the body is deep, folded into a groove and raised when the fish herds small prey into a ball. A slim bill, cobalt back and pale bars that flush and fade with excitement finish the picture. It works the surface of warm, deep ocean by day and all but vanishes at night. Over a short distance almost nothing accelerates harder.
fishdesc.riverfishing.swordfish: The bill is flat and edged like a blade rather than round like a marlin's, and adults carry neither scales nor pelvic fins. Tissue behind the eyes heats brain and retina more than ten degrees above the sea, so vision stays sharp on dives past six hundred metres. After dark it follows squid upward and slashes sideways through them before turning back to feed.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mako: Slate-blue above, chalk-white beneath, with a conical snout and ragged teeth that show even when the jaws are shut. The open sea is its whole range: mid-water over deep, warm and temperate ocean, most active at first light and again at dusk. Warm muscle tissue, rare among sharks, lets it outswim nearly everything that has fins. It leaves the water in long, repeated bounds.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rotan: Squat and dark, with an outsized mouth and a brown-green marbling that lightens or darkens with its mood; spawning males go almost black. It owns the small water - farm ponds, peat cuttings, swamp channels, roadside pools - and empties them of everything living, its own fry included. It survives winters under ice that strip the water of oxygen. Native to the Amur, it now lives across half of Europe.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nase: The mouth is a straight slit under a fleshy snout, edged with a horny lower lip that scrapes algae off stone; the nase makes its living mowing the riverbed. Shoals work gravel runs in clear, quick rivers, always on the bottom, always facing the flow. The lining of the belly is jet black, fair warning of a diet of green stuff and grit. In spring they run upstream to spawn.
fishdesc.riverfishing.vimba: A blunt fleshy snout overhangs the mouth, so the vimba grazes head-down, working larvae and small molluscs out of the gravel. It belongs to running water, cool temperate rivers with a foothold in brackish estuaries, and travels upstream in shoals each spring. Spawning males go coal-black above with an orange-red belly and a rash of white tubercles. It runs hard, then sulks.
fishdesc.riverfishing.smelt: Fresh from the water it smells unmistakably of cucumber, which is how most people identify it before they look. Slim, translucent green over silver, with a big jaw and the small adipose fin that marks its salmonid kin. Shoals hold in cold coastal seas and estuaries after shrimp and small fish, and push into rivers in spring to spawn on sand and gravel. Winter gathers them thickest.
fishdesc.riverfishing.whitefish: Silver and herring-slim, but the small fleshy adipose fin gives away its salmon kinship, and the little mouth sits under a blunt snout for grazing the bottom. Deep cold lakes of the north hold big schools that move onto gravel shallows to spawn in late autumn. It sifts insect larvae, snails and plankton rather than chasing fish. Where water loses its oxygen, this is the first species to go.
fishdesc.riverfishing.char: Dark green back written over with pale worm-track marbling, red spots ringed in blue along the flanks, and lower fins edged white against orange. Cold, clean lakes and mountain streams suit it, and a few fish drop down to brackish water and return heavier. Spawning falls in autumn, when the males turn furnace-orange underneath. Warm water is not merely disliked but fatal.
fishdesc.riverfishing.lenok: Blunt-nosed and small-mouthed for a salmonid, brassy-olive with a scatter of fine dark speckles. Cold mountain and taiga rivers across Siberia and Mongolia are its whole world, and it holds in the quick water below the riffles. It eats whatever moves - insects, fry, the occasional swimming mouse - and keenest of all at first light. It shares those rivers with the taimen, which grows ten times heavier.
fishdesc.riverfishing.taimen: The biggest of the salmon family, a Siberian river fish with an olive head, dark peppering along the flanks and a tail that turns rust-red with age. It holds mid-water in fast taiga and mountain rivers, working the seams below rapids at dawn and dusk. Growth is slow and life long, so a metre-plus fish may be thirty years old. Rodents and swimming birds are fair game.
fishdesc.riverfishing.salmon: Fresh from the sea it is bar-silver, with black x-shaped marks above the lateral line; months in fresh water turn it bronze and give males a curved kype. It feeds at sea and almost stops once it enters the river, running hardest in autumn toward the gravel where it hatched. The way home is found by smell, tributary by tributary. Unlike Pacific salmon, some survive spawning and go back down.
fishdesc.riverfishing.pink_salmon: At sea it is a plain silver fish with tiny scales and large oval spots across the tail. On the spawning run the male grows a grotesque hump and hooked jaws, and both sexes darken and blotch. Its life runs on a strict two-year clock, so odd and even year-classes never meet. After feeding hard through the northern summer it enters the rivers in autumn, spawns and dies.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sturgeon: Five rows of bony scutes down a scaleless body, a shark-like upper tail lobe and four barbels under a pointed snout - a design barely altered in two hundred million years. The mouth slides out like a tube to vacuum worms, molluscs and small fish off riverbeds and estuary sand. It once spawned across half of Europe; one river system, the Garonne and Dordogne, holds the last of it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.halibut: The largest flatfish in the world: both eyes on the right side, the blind underside white, the shape more diamond than oval, a big female running to two and a half metres. It lies on cold deep Atlantic mud, then lifts off to run down cod, haddock and squid - for a flatfish, a formidable swimmer. Growth is slow, and the oldest recorded fish passed fifty.
fishdesc.riverfishing.common_dace: Clean gravel-bottomed rivers, often in hill country, hold shoals of dace, small tidy fish, silver with a greenish back and clean-cut fins. On bright days they lift to the surface and take insects as they drift past. The warm season is their time; in winter they barely show. Dirty water they will not have at all, and where a river fouls the dace goes first.
fishdesc.riverfishing.volga_zander: A smaller cousin of the zander, told apart by the mouth: no dagger-like canines, only even rows of small teeth. Dark bars cross a brassy back, the eye is large, and the cheeks are fully scaled. It keeps to the deep sandy runs of the big rivers of the Volga and Don basins, feeding at dusk and through the night. Autumn is when it shoals and eats hardest.
fishdesc.riverfishing.white_eye_bream: Named for the eye, huge and milky-silver, taking up a good part of the side of the head, and built flat and narrow behind it, with a long anal fin running back to the tail. Deep flowing reaches of big rivers suit it, and it holds on the bottom in current that would push a bream aside. Feeds on larvae and molluscs picked off the sand. Rarely passes a kilo.
fishdesc.riverfishing.round_goby: A blunt-headed bottom fish with eyes set high like a frog's, pelvic fins fused into a sucker for gripping stone, and a black blotch on the rear of the first dorsal fin that settles the identification. It crawls over rubble and shell beds in the Black and Caspian basins and the rivers running into them, crushing molluscs. Nesting males turn coal-black, guard the eggs and die soon after.

guide.riverfishing.tacklebench.title: Tackle bench
guide.riverfishing.tacklebench.text:
The tackle bench crafts custom rigs and lures.
• Pick a FORM (coarse rigs / predator lures), then the WEIGHT - heavier tackle casts farther and costs more iron (1 ingot per 30 g), but must match the rod's cast weight rating.
• Choose the HOOK in the FIRST SLOT - click its left side for smaller, right side for larger (sizes #16 down to #1). You don’t need to provide the hook: the bench ties it directly and charges iron by hook size (in 3-nugget increments per ingot). A #16 adds one ingot, a #4 adds three, and the 3-hook rig pays for all three hooks.
• Materials: iron and string; dye is optional for lures.
• Fine-tuning: hooklink length (rigs) and weight balance (lures) are saved directly onto the finished item.
• Rigs come with hooks pre-installed; each piece is stamped with the crafter's name.

guide.riverfishing.cull.title: The electrofisher: taking out and putting in
guide.riverfishing.cull.text:
The electrofisher changes what a water holds: it takes a species out for good, and it puts in one that was never there. It is a tool for whoever runs the world, not for fishing: it is craftable nowhere and refuses to fire outside creative. Real electrofishing does exactly this job — a crew stuns a stretch of river, removes what does not belong and releases what does.

Right-click water for every species in the mod, laid out by family. Families down the left, one family's fish on the right — and the first category is not a family but THIS WATER, holding what lives here. The coloured strip on a row is its standing: green lives here, red was removed, grey can be put in.

Clicking a row selects it and turns it into a question; a second click on the same row does it. One click is deliberately not enough: a mis-click that empties a lake is not a mistake anyone should be able to make.

## ANY FISH, ANY WATER
There are no gates — it is an admin item, and a marlin goes into a pond if that is what you want. It simply will not be at home there: a species living outside its element sits at a quarter of full activity, present and catchable and never comfortable. That quarter is the whole cost.

## MIND THE SCOPE
A water here is a region of roughly 128 blocks, not the pond you are looking at. Clear roach from one bank and they are gone from the whole region, and a river with several bays is one water. The screen prints the coordinates the region was measured from.

The ban applies everywhere at once: the fish stops biting, vanishes from the shoal you can see in the water, drops off the fish finder and will no longer settle when stocked. That is one check rather than four, so they cannot drift apart. Putting a fish in is the same check from the other side — the species becomes a permanent resident of the region.

Reversible from the screen. A struck-through fish comes back on a second click, where you removed it. Putting fish back in the water does not: a culled species is refused at the bank the way hostile water refuses one, and stays refused until whoever removed it puts it back.

guide.riverfishing.tacklebox.title: Where the tackle lives
guide.riverfishing.tacklebox.text:
Two dozen lines, nine hook sizes, eleven rigs, and dozens of baits - all cluttering your inventory alongside food and building blocks. The tackle box solves that.

Tackle only: line, hooks, rigs, lures, baits, and leaders. No rods or reels - those belong in your hands, not buried in a box.

Four sizes: 9, 18, 27, and 36 slots. Each tier upgrades from the last, with a vanilla chest at the core of every recipe.

Right-click to place it facing you. Sneak + right-click to open it, whether held in hand or placed on the ground: it is the exact same container, sharing inventory, custom name, and color. Breaking the box drops it with all contents intact.

Rename it via the text field at the top of the GUI - no anvil required. Dye the trim with any dye just like leather armor; the contents remain completely untouched. Four boxes with distinct names and colors form your organization system: Pike, Carp, Winter.

The fisherman sells pre-packed kits - float, pike, carp, and saltwater - each named, color-coded, and stocked with bench-crafted tackle. A kit is your complete answer to "what do I need for pike," packed and ready to carry.
guide.riverfishing.keepnet.title: The keepnet: shape decides the room
guide.riverfishing.keepnet.text:
A keepnet is not a chest. Fish take up space based on their actual profile: a meter-long pike takes a narrow strip, while a bream of the same weight forms a squat, wide block. Managing net space is a puzzle, not just filling slots.

Dimensions scale with length and body condition. Each cell represents 25 cm of fish: a 40 cm perch is two cells long, a 90 cm zander is four, and anything exceeding 1.75 m - like a trophy catfish - caps at seven. Width is dictated by Fulton's condition factor: at equal length, a carp is far broader than an asp, as reflected in the grid. A deep-bodied fish three cells wide and four long loses its corner cells, tapering naturally at the snout and tail.

Four tiers available: 5×3, 7×4, 8×5, and 9×6. Each higher tier upgrades from the previous one.

Controls: Right-click the net in hand to open. Pick up a fish and press R to rotate it. Shift-click inserts a fish into the best available opening. TIDY repacks the entire net from scratch, fitting the largest and most awkward specimens first - wasted space can usually be recovered. EMPTY dumps the whole catch straight into your inventory.

Holds only fish from this mod - no tackle, blocks, or food. Tackle belongs in the tackle box.

Available from the fisherman: small at level 3, medium OR large at level 4 (determined per villager), and huge at level 5.

guide.riverfishing.icefishing.title: Ice fishing
guide.riverfishing.icefishing.text:
A winter rod cannot be cast. At all. Point it at open water and it will tell you directly: it fishes straight down through an ice hole, and nowhere else.

## THE AUGER
Right-click ice with it: regular, packed, blue, or frosted, provided there is WATER UNDERNEATH. This cuts a fishing hole and costs one point of the auger's 64 durability.

An ice hole remains as slippery as the surrounding sheet, MELTS UNDER BRIGHT LIGHT just like ice blocks, and breaking it leaves a water source, never ice. Drill where it will last. It is not permanent: step more than four blocks away in freezing weather and the hole skins over - within a few minutes, solid ice returns.

## AN ICE HOLE MEANS WINTER
While you fish an ice hole, the game engine treats the local season as winter regardless of the calendar date. Find ice in July and the fish beneath act as if it were January - which is why walking out for burbot and smelt is well worth the trip.

## JIGGING TECHNIQUE
The first right-click drops the mormyshka into the water; subsequent clicks jig the lure. A STEADY cadence - one twitch every 0.4 to 1.0 s - advances the bite timer by 34 ticks. Ragged or sluggish jigging advances it by only 8 ticks. That is a fourfold difference, and during the wait, cadence is the only factor in your hands.
A mormyshka is not the only option for the tackle slot. A dash in the table means that species ignores jigs completely: burbot demands worms, liver, or live baitfish, and the winter rig accepts all three.

## THE BITE
There is no bite audio cue, no "Bite!" text popup, and the tip of the rod will not dip. Instead, the water inside the hole boils with a sudden burst of bubbles and spray - that is your sole strike indicator. Hookset just as you would with any other rod.

Snags are practically nonexistent. A line suspended vertically down an ice hole has far fewer obstacles to catch on than one cast across an open lake.

guide.riverfishing.nets.title: Nets
guide.riverfishing.nets.text:
A rod takes one fish, and it takes the one that was hungry. A net scoops everything at once: the fish you wanted, the fish you did not, and the broodstock that would have spawned next spring. Drag a seine through a pond in March and there will be no April in it - that water stays empty for years, not just for an evening.

## WHY ANGLERS ARE FORBIDDEN FROM USING NETS
This is why nets are banned for sport anglers everywhere, and why in this mod netting water you did not stock is pure poaching. The haul still succeeds - a net that failed completely would teach nothing. But every fisherman within earshot witnesses the crime: contract reputation drops by 5 points, and the local fish population depletes TWICE as fast as the catch itself accounts for, because future generations were wiped out with it. This debt is real and scales into the NEGATIVE: drop below zero and the trusted trade tier locks; drop 15 points below and the contract board goes completely blank. Time will not heal it, and emeralds cannot buy forgiveness. To recover 1 point, release 5 kg of mature fish back into WILD water - restocking your private pond does not count, as those fish remain yours and offer nothing to the village.

## WHOSE WATER IT IS
A net belongs in the hands of a fish farmer on private water. Water you stocked yourself - an established breeding pair or stocked fingerlings - is yours to harvest, and a claimed pond is entirely your property regardless of what the field guide says about local species. Here, nets serve their true purpose: a seine hauls 1–3 fish per minute with 64 uses of durability, a cast net yields at most one fish every 15 seconds and tears after 32 throws, and within your claimed claim boundary the cooldown between hauls drops to a third of standard time - the water is being cultivated, not pillaged. However, every netted catch permanently bears the tag NETTED, and catches from unowned water are marked POACHED. That label can never be removed.

Everywhere else, use a rod.
guide.riverfishing.stocking.title: Stocking a water
guide.riverfishing.stocking.text:
A body of water keeps what you put in it. Release a fish, and it is recorded in that water’s ledger - one ledger per ~128-block sector, not just the single pond before you.

## THE BROODSTOCK

One mature female and one mature male, or thirty fry; the info card specifies what you are holding. Marginal water will accept the broodstock but never let the species settle permanently; hostile water rejects the release immediately and explains why.

## THE WAIT

The broodstock must survive an ENTIRE spawning window - 24 days, or 8 for a sub-season. A window that is already in progress does not count, pushing the timer to the following year. The release prompt acts as a checklist: sexes, suitability, and days remaining. Catch the breeding pair early and the timer resets; on the final day, the species settles for good, and half the fry mature into full-sized fish.

## YOUR OWN POND

A sign placed within three blocks of water claims that body (up to 600 blocks) - an artificial pit or a village pond, but never a river. Wild fish will not spawn, restrictions on depth, width, biome, and province are lifted, and using your own net becomes legal. Break the sign, and the water turns wild again.

## POACHING

Casting a net in water you never stocked costs five fisherman reputation points and depletes the population at double speed. Three illegal hauls from a clean slate will wipe the contract board clean. The only road to redemption is releasing five kilograms of mature fish into WILD water per point recovered - fish placed into your private pond remain yours.

guide.riverfishing.breeding.title: The breeding tank
guide.riverfishing.breeding.text:
Fish spawn once a year, during one third of a single season - eight days out of ninety-six. A breeding tank cannot shift that schedule; it only gives you full environmental control while the window is open.

## THE PAIR
The largest adult ♀ and a compatible adult ♂ of her species or a close relative (sazan and carp share the same taxonomy). Both require an angler's catch card; netted fish carry no recorded sex and cannot be bred.

## THREE UNBROKEN DAYS
Active season, fully fed, and water level above 50%% - all three conditions must be met continuously every day. A missed feeding resets progress to zero, wasting any fish oil applied. Fish oil and a gravel substrate each shave off one day; the duration cannot drop below a 24-hour minimum.

## THE CLUTCH
An average hen carries about 25 eggs; one twice that size caps out at 40. Breeding two leather carp carrying the lethal homozygous naked allele immediately costs 25%% of the clutch, as double-recessive eggs fail to develop.

## THE ROE
Eggs and adult fish cannot share a tank: the adults will not eat the roe, but incubation halts entirely. Remove the breeders to resume incubation: 4 days in the species' native climate, 8 days in non-native conditions. Progress pauses if water drops below 25%%. Hatch rates scale with egg vitality, ranging from 90%% down to 50%%.

## RETURNING FRY TO WATER
Fingerlings are dropped as items: toss them into the water and let them float for two seconds. In open, barren water, only 7 in 10 survive; adding submerged snags and an aerator raises fry survival to 19 in 20.

guide.riverfishing.genes.title: Genes and varieties
guide.riverfishing.genes.text:
Hold Shift on a landed fish and the card reveals its genetics: Ss Cc VV ff. S size, C color, V vigor, F fertility - one allele pair each, dominant capitalized and listed first. These are functional mechanics, not cosmetic tags. An established all-SS stock yields fish at 1.15× standard weight, while an all-ss stock yields 0.90×; dominant color doubles the chance of rare morphs; VV roe survives incubation 9 times out of 10, whereas vv survives only half the time; FF females spawn 1.5× more eggs. A blank card indicates homozygous recessive across all traits - an average fish, never a hidden champion.

## THE CARP'S SCALES
Carp carry two additional allele pairs: K (scaled, dominant over k mirror) and N (linear/nude, dominant over n normal).

NN is a lethal gene. A homozygous leather pair immediately loses 25%% of its clutch, meaning the leather variety can never be genetically stabilized - that risk is the cost of breeding it.

## THE KOI
Koi express five extra loci: W white base, R red pattern, B black markings, G metallic luster, and T the crown. There are 17 distinct varieties, determined top-down - the first qualifying rule defines the phenotype. Tancho is the recessive tt on a kohaku - a single red crown and nothing else - and it comes only from a tancho line: a kohaku pair cannot produce one. A koi from the water is pure at its base and its luster, so kohaku from kohaku is always kohaku - never a dark-based or a metallic fish; at the red and the black it is a mongrel, and the card shows it (Rr, Bb) - which is where a kohaku line drops the odd shiro muji and a sanke drops a bekko. Pick parents that read pure on the card and the line breeds true; cross two lines and the second generation sorts itself by Mendel. Only 9 of the 17 varieties occur in the wild; the remaining 8 - including tancho and metallic yamabuki - must be selectively bred. Metallic sheen enters a pond only via wild kujaku or gin bekko (1 in 13 wild koi).

## HYBRIDIZATION
Eight genetic pools determine clutch viability modifiers: carp, sazan, and koi are biologically identical (1.0 factor); both crucian carp species likewise (1.0); sturgeons (0.8); salmon, trout, and char (0.5); bream with white bream (0.9), but with other cyprinids (0.2). The silver crucian carp never truly hybridizes: foreign milt merely triggers gynogenetic division of the egg, producing direct clones of the mother.

## THE PATTERN INDEX
Every carp and koi rolls a pattern seed from 0 to 999 across 12 families of variable width. A seed's exact placement within its band further modulates pigment distribution - two kohaku of identical weight remain visually unique. Twelve exact integers produce solid-color prize morphs: uniform coverage, 6× trade value, appearing once in 83 catches. Pattern seeds are heritable with continuous variance, meaning a bloodline drifts toward a family without ever locking onto a fixed number.

guide.riverfishing.upgrades.title: Building the water
guide.riverfishing.upgrades.text:
Five blocks, and none does anything right where it sits. Each places a MARK on the water: place one, and every cast within 24 blocks horizontally (and six blocks up or down) fishes over improved water. A second aerator is merely a second block, not a stacking bonus.

## SUBMERGED OR BANKSIDE
The Aerator, Snag Pile, and Gravel Bed are waterlogged blocks placed directly on the bottom. The other two cannot hold water: placing either into a water source leaves a dry air pocket where the water was.

## BUBBLES AND BRUSH
An aerator slightly clears the water, prompting sight predators - pike, asp, perch, chub, trout - to feed nearly 25%% harder year-round; the summer oxygen boost stacks on top. A snag pile provides essential cover: predators hold tight to it, and wild fry use it for shelter.

## GRAVEL CUTS BOTH WAYS
A gravel bed forces the entire swim to register as gravel, regardless of the natural bottom substrate. Salmonids bite 20%% more eagerly over it and predators gain a 12.5%% boost - but carp seek out silt and sturgeon want sand, both of which are wiped out.

## THE FEEDER STATION
Add groundbait via right-click: one jar supplies four in-game days, the hopper stores eight jars, and one jar depletes per day while the model visibly tracks remaining stock. Kept fed, the swim yields a ×1.6 bite modifier, 25%% shorter wait times, and 25%% faster weight gain per season for stocked fish. It does not dictate WHO visits - that is decided strictly by the mix thrown by hand.

All five blocks double as aquarium modules, which is the primary purpose of the Warm Outflow: in open water, it only shifts local thermometer readings and little else.

guide.riverfishing.geography.title: Half a planet
guide.riverfishing.geography.text:
Minecraft has weather, not geography: identical swamps, taigas, and jungles repeat all the way to the world border, so any fish gated only by climate would thrive everywhere that climate matches. Instead, world generation carves the map into four faunal provinces - organic regions roughly 3,000 blocks across, fixed forever by the seed.

## ABSENT, NOT RARE
Each species lists the provinces where it belongs and is completely absent from the rest, no matter how perfect the water looks. Not rarer, not smaller: entirely absent. The ocean remains undivided - one sea, one global fauna - as are fish that humans have spread worldwide: 37 species belong to no single province.

## BIOME SPECIALISTS
A common fish settles for the best among its acceptable biomes. Sixteen specialists demand multiple biomes at once, strictly without compromise: taimen requires cold rivers, arapaima needs warm jungles, and snakehead wants warm swamps. Meeting only half the criteria yields nothing.

## READING THE DATA
The fish finder displays the current province directly beneath the water body name, both on the main display and on the water card. On the chart, scroll the mouse wheel to zoom out: once the view spans roughly 1,000 blocks, provincial borders appear beneath the water - four distinct patterns, gold boundary lines, and the center province named in the corner.

## TWO WAYS AROUND IT
Travel to the fish, or bring it to you: a claimed pond completely bypasses regional gates, and an introduced species established outside its native range still lives on at 25%% base strength.
