fishdesc.riverfishing.koi_carp: The parent stock behind every named variety: an amur carp bred for colour, heavy through the body, with four barbels at the mouth and scaling that may be full, mirrored or absent altogether. Colours run from plain white through orange and gold to black in any combination. A century of pond life has made these fish slow to spook, but a startled eight-kilo carp leaves the shallows in one burst.

fishdesc.riverfishing.aba_aba: A long ribbon of a fish with no tail fin, no pelvics and no anal fin - motion comes from a single dorsal that undulates along most of the back and drives it forward or backward with equal ease. It reads the muddy Nile, Niger and Chad basins through its own weak electric field, hunting fish after dark where eyes are useless. Adults weave floating grass nests a metre across.
fishdesc.riverfishing.adonis_pleco: Enamel bristles called odontodes cover the fins and flanks of this metre-long armoured catfish and will open a careless hand. Black, sown with white spots that fade as it grows, it clings to rock and sunken wood in fast Amazon tributaries, rasping algae, wood and carrion off hard surfaces. It works at night and spends the day wedged in a crevice, driving other bottom fish off its stone.
fishdesc.riverfishing.african_arowana: Despite the name and the bony-tongued lineage, this one is a filter feeder: a spiral organ in the throat strains plankton and detritus out of the water it gulps at the surface. Heavy-bodied and bronze-brown, it reaches a metre and ten kilos in floodplain swamps, backwaters and marshy ponds across West and Central Africa. A pair tramples a walled nest in the grass and shepherds the fry.
fishdesc.riverfishing.african_knifefish: Brown and shaped like a blade, it has no dorsal fin: the long anal fin runs unbroken to the tail tip and ripples to hold the fish nose-down or slide it backwards. It spends the day among roots and leaf litter in shaded West African swamp creeks, coming out at dusk for larvae, worms and small fish. It also barks, forcing air from the swim bladder.
fishdesc.riverfishing.african_pike_chara: Not a pike but a characin dressed as one: pointed head, dorsal set far back, and long conical teeth that show even with the jaws shut. It hangs motionless in mid-water among reeds and drowned branches of West African rivers, then takes prey in one short lunge. Dawn and dusk are its hours, and the pair guards a foam nest until the fry swim.
fishdesc.riverfishing.african_sharptooth: A flattened, spade-shaped head, tiny eyes, four pairs of barbels and an eel-like body reaching nearly two metres and sixty kilos. A branched organ above the gills lets it breathe air, cross wet ground to the next pool and sit out a drought in mud. After dark it searches the bottom of swamps, floodplains and turbid rivers for fish, frogs, snails and anything else. It fights by going straight down.
fishdesc.riverfishing.alligator_gar: Three metres and a hundred and fifty kilos of living armour, plated in interlocking ganoid scales, with a broad snout and two rows of teeth in the upper jaw. It idles at the surface of oxbows, bayous and flooded backwaters of the lower Mississippi, gulping air through a swim bladder that works as a lung. Prey is taken in a sideways slash. The roe is poisonous to mammals.
fishdesc.riverfishing.angolan_clarias: No longer than a forearm, which makes it modest company beside its two-metre relatives. Dark olive-brown above and pale below, with long barbels and the same unbroken fin running back to the tail. It keeps to weedy swamp channels, floodplain pools and shaded stretches of Congo basin rivers, working the bottom after dark for insect larvae, worms and small fish. Like the rest of its family it breathes air.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ansorges_dwarf_cha: Barely the length of a thumbnail, this striped mite of a characin carries a row of dark blotches down each silver flank and a pale belly. It works the middle water of warm African forest streams, quiet pools, swamp edges and rain-filled hollows, dropping to clean sand between darts. Insect larvae and tiny crustaceans are the whole of its diet. Daylight is its working shift; after dark it hangs motionless.
fishdesc.riverfishing.asian_arowana: Big enamelled scales, a chin tilted upward like a drawbridge and two stiff barbels mark the dragonfish of Southeast Asia. It patrols the surface film of blackwater swamps, forest rivers and flooded backwaters, taking insects, frogs and small fish with a lunge that can carry it clear of the water and into the branches. The male broods the eggs in his mouth until the young swim off on their own.
fishdesc.riverfishing.barramundi: Wedge-shaped and silver, sloping of forehead, with eyes that flare red in a torch beam. It shifts between coastal rivers, lakes and estuaries of northern Australia and Southeast Asia, feeding hardest at first and last light, when it herds mullet against a bank. Every barramundi begins life as a male and turns female with age, so the giants are all mothers. Alarmed, it bolts along the surface in tail-walking leaps.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bester_sturgeon: A made fish rather than a wild one: beluga crossed with sterlet, first raised in Soviet ponds in the 1950s. The beluga gave it bulk and greedy growth, the sterlet early maturity and a life spent wholly in fresh water. Five rows of bony scutes armour the back, and four barbels sweep the river bed for worms, molluscs and drowned insects. It feeds from dusk through the night.
fishdesc.riverfishing.black_crappie: Irregular dark speckling over a silver-green side, without vertical bars, and seven or eight spines in the dorsal fin separate it from its white cousin. Schools hang in mid-water around drowned brush and weed edges in clear lakes and slow rivers, feeding at dawn and dusk on minnows and insect larvae. Spring brings whole colonies of nests to the shallows. Old-timers call it calico bass for the mottling.
fishdesc.riverfishing.black_drum: Oysters and crabs go down whole, shell and all: a set of pharyngeal millstones in the throat grinds them, and a short bristle of chin barbels finds them in the sand. Young fish wear four or five vertical bars that fade to plain slate with age. Males croak with the swim bladder, a groan that carries through a hull. Sixty-year-olds of fifty kilograms still work the surf and channel edges.
fishdesc.riverfishing.black_mahseer: Coin-sized scales, thick rubbery lips and a slate back over brassy flanks belong to the mahseer of the Western Ghats. It holds on the bottom of boulder rivers and hill reservoirs, grinding down fallen fruit, algae, snails and whatever the monsoon sweeps in. Sixteen kilograms of muscle in heavy current gives ground slowly. In temple pools on the southern rivers these fish are fed by hand and never harmed.
fishdesc.riverfishing.black_white_crappi: Cross a black crappie with a white one and the speckling comes out muddled, half-remembering the bars of the white parent. The deep body belongs to the black side of the family, the quick growth and taste for cloudy water to the other. Schools hang in mid-water over sunken brush, picking off fry and larvae. Breeding is poor, which is precisely why ponds get stocked with them.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blacktail_snapper: Yellow-brown above and pale below, with lemon fins and the dark smudge on the tail that gave the fish its name. It hangs about reef edges, lagoons and the surf zone from East Africa to the Pacific islands, running down small fish, crabs and shrimp in short rushes. Days are busy, nights are spent wedged into coral. Hawaii took it in during the 1950s and never got rid of it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blotched_upsidedow: Most of its life is spent belly-up, and the colouring follows suit: the belly is dark, the back pale, countershading turned on its head. This small mottled synodontis of the Congo basin scrapes midge and mosquito larvae off the underside of the surface film and off sunken timber. Days pass in shade under logs; feeding begins at dusk. Handled roughly, it creaks with the spines of its pectoral fins.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blue_catfish: Slate-blue back, white belly and a tail forked as deeply as a swallow's: the largest catfish in North America, good for sixty-eight kilograms. It lies up in the channels of big rivers and reservoirs and works the bottom after dark for shad, mussels and drowned carrion. A straight-edged anal fin with thirty-odd rays tells it from the channel cat. Brackish estuaries bother it not at all.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blue_mozambique_ti: The cross was made for ponds: cold hardiness from the blue parent, fast growth and an easy way with salty water from the Mozambique side. Colour lands in between, a dusky body with a reddish edge to the tail in ripe males. It grazes algae, detritus and plankton in warm shallow ponds, lakes and swamp margins. Hybrid or not, the female still carries eggs and fry in her mouth.
fishdesc.riverfishing.blue_tilapia: Steel-blue over the head, pink-red trim along the dorsal and tail, and a spawning male dark enough to look purple. Of all the tilapias this one stands cold the best, staying active in water that finishes off its relatives, which is how it spread far beyond the Nile. It rasps algae and strains plankton in shallow lakes and swamps. Males dig saucer nests; females carry the eggs in the mouth.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluegill_green_sun: Green sunfish supplies the wide mouth, the heavy head and the temper; bluegill the deep plate of a body and long pointed pectorals. The result wears turquoise worm-lines across the cheek and a black ear tab, grows quickly and comes out almost entirely male. Weedy pond margins and quiet bays suit it, where it hoovers insects, snails and fry from mid-water. Spring nests crowd together on gravel.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluegill_pumpkinse: Two parents that nest side by side on the same shallows produce this fish often enough for it to have earned a nickname. The pumpkinseed contributes the orange crescent on the ear flap and wavy blue lines across the cheek, the bluegill the dark blotch at the back of the dorsal fin. Small even for the family, it picks snails, larvae and crustaceans out of pondweed.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluegill_redbreast: The ear flap gives the game away: longer and narrower than a bluegill's and solid black, yet not the thin ribbon a redbreast carries. Below it the belly runs orange, another gift from the redbreast, while the deep round body comes from the other parent. It favours slack river edges and warm ponds with wood and weed to hide in. Insects, snails and small crayfish fill out the year.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bluegill_redear_hy: Redear hands down the crushing throat plates that let a sunfish live on snails, plus the scarlet rim of the ear flap; bluegill the round deep body and the black tag on the dorsal fin. The cross outgrows both parents and reaches thirty-five centimetres in a fertile pond. It works mid-water and weed edges in eastern lakes and ponds. Spring finds it fanning nests on warm sand.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bowfin: Little about this fish has changed since the Jurassic: a bony plate under the jaw, a long undulating dorsal fin down most of the back, and a swim bladder used as a lung in water too foul for anything else. The male wears a black eyespot ringed in orange and shepherds a squirming ball of fry for weeks. He hunts the bottom of swamps after dark, and bites with conviction.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bream_roach_hybrid: Neither one thing nor the other: the back is high but never the steep slab of a bream, the anal fin shorter, the eye and lower fins red as a roach's. Bream and roach shed their eggs over the same flooded grass in the same week, so the cross turns up wherever both live. It grubs lake beds for bloodworm and molluscs, and rarely leaves offspring of its own.
fishdesc.riverfishing.brook_bull_trout_h: Where brook trout were let loose in bull trout country the two chars interbreed, and the young come out sterile, a quiet way of emptying a river of its native fish. The heavy head and pale spots come from the bull trout, the worm-tracked back and white-edged fins from the brookie. It holds in cold streams and lakes, eats insects and small fish, and runs in short hard bursts.
fishdesc.riverfishing.brook_trout: Marbled worm-tracks across an olive back, red dots each set in a blue halo, clean white edges on the lower fins: the only char most people ever meet. Cold spring creeks, headwaters and mountain lakes are its whole world, and warm water kills it faster than any predator. Autumn turns the males orange along the belly and drives them onto gravel. Insects go down in a fast, splashy rise.
fishdesc.riverfishing.bull_trout: No black anywhere in the dorsal fin, and pale yellow and rose spots over an olive flank: so this char is told from the trout it shares a river with. It demands the coldest, cleanest water going, and travels a hundred kilometres upriver to reach spawning gravel in autumn. Big ones live on fish, taking sculpins and young salmon from ambush. A metre and fourteen kilograms is the ceiling.
fishdesc.riverfishing.cameroon_suckermou: Under the rush of a Cameroon hill stream, a catfish the length of a finger joint clamps to bare rock with a fleshy oral disc and stays put. The name polypogon, many beards, is for the crowd of short barbels ringing that disc, which feel out midge larvae and algal film on the stone. Flattened head, low body, nothing for the current to catch. Grazing happens at night.
fishdesc.riverfishing.catla: A head taking up nearly a third of the body, a jutting lower jaw and broad silvery scales make this Indian carp hard to mistake. Warm rivers and lakes across the monsoon lands hold it, where it works soft, silty ground in slow water. Growth is extravagant, and a hundred kilograms has been recorded. In a fight it pulls with a dull persistence that never quite ends.
fishdesc.riverfishing.chain_pickerel: Down each green flank runs a chain-link pattern, and a dark bar drops below the eye like a smudge of soot. Weedy lakes and quiet ponds of eastern North America suit it best, where it hangs motionless in mid-water among the stems. Cold does not slow it; autumn and the half-light of dawn and dusk are its hours. The strike is one short burst, then a scramble of jumps.
fishdesc.riverfishing.channel_blue_catfi: From the channel catfish come the scattered dark spots of youth and a broad, undiscriminating appetite; from the blue come the heavy build, the flat back and the long anal fin with its straight edge. The cross outgrows both parents and reaches twenty kilos in rivers and larger lakes. It feeds after dark, close to the bottom. Alarmed, it goes down and stays down.
fishdesc.riverfishing.chinese_mahseer: Thick rubbery lips and scales far too large for a forty-centimetre fish mark out the smallest of the mahseers. Its water is the cold upper rivers of Yunnan and the Mekong headwaters, tumbling through gorges and jungle valleys over stone. At first and last light it picks insects and small fish from among the boulders; winter shuts it down almost completely. For its size, few river fish pull harder.
fishdesc.riverfishing.chinook_coho_hybri: Blood from two Pacific salmon meets here: the deep shoulders, black gums and sheer weight of the king, and the bright silver and upper-lobe-only tail spotting of the coho. The result is a middling fish, heavier than a coho and livelier than a chinook. It puts on its growth at sea and climbs cold rivers in autumn. Long runs end with the fish skidding across the surface.
fishdesc.riverfishing.chinook_pink_hybri: Where a king and a humpback interbreed, the offspring carries the pink's fine scales and large oval spots on both lobes of the tail alongside the chinook's dark mouth and longer frame. Ninety centimetres is about the ceiling, well beyond any pure pink salmon. Autumn brings it out of the sea and into cold northern rivers. It runs fast and shallow, leaving a long wake behind it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.chinook_salmon: Heaviest of the Pacific salmon, the king wears black gums at the base of its teeth and heavy spotting over the back and both lobes of the tail. Record fish have approached sixty kilos, though half that is already the fish of a season. It winters at sea and climbs cold rivers in autumn, pressing further inland than any relative. Its runs are long, deep and slow to end.
fishdesc.riverfishing.chum_salmon: In fresh water the flanks flare into ragged purple and green bars, and males grow the canines that earned the name dog salmon. No neat black spots break the pattern; it is smeared, almost tiger-striped. From Kamchatka to Alaska it leans hard on the sea, returning in autumn, and some fish push thousands of kilometres up the Yukon and the Amur. The fight is broad-shouldered rather than acrobatic.
fishdesc.riverfishing.climbing_perch: Spiny gill covers, a stocky brown body and a labyrinth organ let this small Asian fish leave the water altogether and shuffle across wet ground from a drying pool to the next one. Swamps, ditches, ponds and monsoon puddles are its world, and heat is its season. It hunts insects and scraps in mid-water through the day. Buried in mud, it can wait out weeks of drought.
fishdesc.riverfishing.coho_salmon: White gums under a dark tongue, spots on the back and on the upper lobe of the tail only, and in spawning dress a flank the colour of old wine. Autumn takes it into small coastal rivers and their lake systems, often later than any other salmon. The sea years put on the weight, up to fifteen kilos. Of the Pacific salmon, this is the one that jumps.
fishdesc.riverfishing.common_barbel: Four fleshy barbels hang around a downturned mouth, and the body is a bronze torpedo built for gravel and current. Clean, oxygen-rich rivers hold it, and at dawn and dusk it turns over stones for larvae and snails. Spring sends shoals upstream to spawn on shallow gravel, and the roe at that season is poisonous, a lesson usually learned once. Its resistance is low, dogged and drawn out.
fishdesc.riverfishing.common_carp_gibel_: Two unlike cyprinids meet in this fish: the carp lends a deep body, fast growth and a trace of barbels, often worn down to stubs, while the gibel carp lends a short head, a tough constitution and indifference to stale, airless water. Ponds, lakes and weedy backwaters are its home. Feeding is steady along the bottom, never hurried. Most individuals are sterile and simply keep putting on weight.
fishdesc.riverfishing.congo_knifefish: Shaped like a blade, this Congo featherback swims by rippling one long anal fin and travels backwards as neatly as forwards. Dark brown skin flecked with pale dots hides it among flooded forest, swamp margins and slow side channels. Night is its feeding time, when it comes out of cover and takes small fish with a single lunge. Its swim bladder doubles as a lung.
fishdesc.riverfishing.cornish_jack: Largest of the elephantfish, this African oddity is eel-bodied, blunt-snouted and dull grey-brown, and reads the darkness with a weak electric field of its own making. Rivers and lakes of the Congo and Zambezi hold it, down among snags and sunken timber. After dusk it hunts in packs, a rare habit in fresh water, driving small cichlids against cover. Fifteen kilos is a grown adult.
fishdesc.riverfishing.crimean_barbel: A slimmer, darker relative of the common barbel, with faint dusky blotches along the back and seventy centimetres for a ceiling. Its whole world is a handful of short, cold rivers running off the Crimean mountains to the Black Sea. It works gravel runs for larvae and small fish at dawn and dusk, and spawns on shallows in spring. So narrow a range makes it a genuinely scarce fish.
fishdesc.riverfishing.cutbow: Fertile, unlike most crosses between species, and that is the trouble: where rainbow and cutthroat ranges meet in the American west, pure cutthroat stocks dissolve into hybrids. The throat slash fades to a smudge here, laid over the pink lateral stripe and fine spotting of the rainbow parent. Cold mountain rivers and lakes hold it, at its best through autumn. It jumps like one parent and sulks like the other.
fishdesc.riverfishing.cutthroat_trout: Two crimson slashes under the lower jaw give the fish its name and are usually the first thing anyone notices. Black spotting crowds toward the tail over an olive or brassy body, and the pattern shifts with every subspecies, from desert lakes to coastal streams. Sea-run and lake forms grow heavy, the largest on record near nineteen kilos. A trusting nature has cost this trout dearly.
fishdesc.riverfishing.desert_pupfish: Barely seven centimetres long, this survivor of the American southwest turns iridescent blue with an orange tail in breeding males and stays a plain olive the rest of the year. Springs, seeps, marsh pools and shrinking puddles are its habitat, warm and often saltier than the sea. It grazes algae and larvae in the shallows through the hottest hours. Water at forty degrees does not trouble it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.devils_hole_pupfis: One flooded limestone cavern in the Nevada desert is the entire range of this fish, and a single shallow rock shelf inside it serves as both spawning ground and pantry. The fish itself is blue, big-eyed, and lacks pelvic fins altogether, three and a half centimetres from nose to tail. The water sits near thirty-three degrees and holds little oxygen. In bad years the whole species has numbered under forty.
fishdesc.riverfishing.dolly_bull_trout_h: Both parents are chars, so the offspring carries pale cream and rose spots on a dark olive ground and never a black one. The bull trout supplies the broad flat head, the wide jaw and the taste for other fish; the Dolly Varden supplies a rounder body and a readiness to drop down to salt water. Cold mountain rivers of the Pacific northwest hold it. It strikes hard and short.
fishdesc.riverfishing.dolly_varden: Small pink and cream spots, none of them larger than the pupil, scatter over an olive back that reddens as autumn comes on. Cold rivers and lakes around the North Pacific hold it, from Kamchatka to Alaska, and many fish run to the sea and back. Young ones eat insects; older ones turn to fish and to salmon eggs. The name came from a Dickens character in a spotted dress.
fishdesc.riverfishing.double_nose_elepha: A long trunk-like snout curves down from the head, flexible enough to probe into crevices, and the fish reads its surroundings through a weak electric field rather than by eye. Channels and flooded forest of the Congo suit it, where it turns over silt after dark for insect larvae. Twenty-two centimetres counts as a big one. Its brain, measured against body weight, rivals a mammal's.
fishdesc.riverfishing.eastern_happy: Males in condition glow yellow-gold and blue, with a row of egg-coloured spots along the anal fin; females stay a speckled bronze. Lake Malawi's weedy margins suit this cichlid, and so do the streams and swamps feeding it. By day it picks insects from mid-water, and the female broods her eggs in her mouth. Geneticists call it the nearest living stand-in for the ancestor of the whole Malawi swarm.
fishdesc.riverfishing.electric_catfish: A soft grey sausage of a fish, thickly speckled, with no dorsal fin at all and three pairs of barbels ringing a blunt mouth. It passes the African day wedged under sunken timber in warm swamps and slow ponds, then works the bottom from dusk until dawn. Nearly the whole body is a living battery, and a discharge of several hundred volts stuns whatever it decides to swallow.
fishdesc.riverfishing.electric_eel: Not an eel at all but a giant South American knifefish: a cylindrical body two and a half metres long, dark above, dull orange at the throat, driven by one long rippling fin along the belly. Muddy backwaters and flooded forest in the Amazon basin suit it, and it must rise for air every few minutes to breathe. Three electric organs deliver the strongest shock any animal produces.
fishdesc.riverfishing.elephantnose_fish: The trunk is really a flexible extension of the chin, studded with electroreceptors and used to probe soft mud for insect larvae. Weak pulses from an organ in the tail map a river bottom the eyes can barely make out, and the brain, measured against body weight, is among the largest of any fish. It keeps to slow, tannin-dark rivers of West Africa, sheltering by day and feeding after dusk.
fishdesc.riverfishing.elongate_lamprolog: Built like a small pike - long, silver-grey, pointed in the head, with the fins set well back - this Tanganyikan cichlid hangs in midwater over rock and sand. Shoals of young cichlids are its living, run down in daylight with a single burst across the last metre. A pair will hold a stretch of shoreline and drive everything away from the cloud of their own fry.
fishdesc.riverfishing.fierce_bathybates: Silver flanks carrying rows of dark blotches, a large eye and jaws full of fine needle teeth all point one way: this is a hunter of sardines in open water. It ranges over the offshore depths of Lake Tanganyika, lifting into the middle layers behind shoals of clupeids and taking them in short sprints by day. For a fish under forty centimetres, the name fierce is generously given.
fishdesc.riverfishing.flathead_catfish: No other North American catfish looks quite so surly: flat head, squared-off tail, and a lower jaw that juts well past the upper over mottled olive-and-yellow hide. Big rivers are its country, where it spends daylight jammed into a logjam or a deep undercut bank and comes out after dark. It wants living fish and takes carrion rarely; the heaviest weighed have passed fifty kilograms.
fishdesc.riverfishing.flier: Almost circular in profile, with dorsal and anal fins so nearly matched that the fish looks ready to glide away from the water. Rows of small dark spots run along olive flanks, and a dark bar drops from the eye like a smudged tear. Acidic swamps, backwaters and weedy ponds of the American southeast are its ground. Young fish carry a false eyespot on the dorsal fin.
fishdesc.riverfishing.florida_gar: Dark round blotches scatter over the head, body and fins of this long, cigar-shaped predator, whose snout is broader and shorter than in its northern relatives. The armour is a mail of hard enamelled diamond scales that little can bite through. It hangs motionless near the surface of weedy Florida swamps and canals, gulping air when the water turns stale, and takes small fish with a fast sideways slash.
fishdesc.riverfishing.frontosa_cichlid: Old males carry a fatty hump that swells over the forehead until the whole fish looks top-heavy; beneath it, six black bars cross a chalky blue-white body. Its ground is the deeper rocky shelves of Lake Tanganyika, where it moves without hurry until a smaller cichlid drifts within range of one short rush. Females brood the eggs in the mouth for weeks and go hungry throughout.
fishdesc.riverfishing.giant_cichlid: The largest cichlid in the world is also one of the plainest: a silvery, small-scaled fish shaped like an overgrown perch, with a reddish flush in the tail. Pairs settle on the sandy shelves of Lake Tanganyika and shepherd clouds of several thousand fry across open bottom. Adults chase down smaller fish in short rushes, and most appear to spawn only once before dying.
fishdesc.riverfishing.giant_featherback: A blade of a fish: humped back, deep compressed body, a dorsal fin reduced to a small feather, and one long fin running the whole underside from throat to tail. The wave along that fin travels either way, so it can back out of a snag without turning around. It hunts smaller fish through flooded forest and slow Sundaland rivers after dark, and the Javan population may already be gone.
fishdesc.riverfishing.giant_freshwater_s: Buried to the eyes in Mekong sand, it gives nothing away until the bottom lifts: an oval brown disc more than two metres across, pale beneath, trailing a whip of a tail armed with a serrated spine as long as a forearm. Clams and small fish are located by electric sense rather than sight. The heaviest reach half a tonne and grip the riverbed like a suction cup.
fishdesc.riverfishing.giant_gourami: Deep-bodied and heavy, with a forehead that grows almost square in old fish and pelvic fins drawn out into long feeling threads. A labyrinth organ lets it breathe air, so it thrives in warm, stagnant swamps and ponds where oxygen runs thin. Adults turn largely vegetarian, grazing water plants and fallen fruit, and a pair weaves a ball of plant fibre to hold the eggs.
fishdesc.riverfishing.giant_mottled_eel: No other freshwater eel ranges so widely, from Mozambique across to the Pacific islands and north to Japan, and none is so heavily marked: dark olive clouds marble a thick snake of a body up to two metres long. Elvers climb wet rock beside waterfalls to reach headwater pools. Adults lie under stones through the day and quarter the bottom at night, then leave for the open ocean to spawn.
fishdesc.riverfishing.giant_snakehead: Juveniles are brilliant orange-red and swarm in a ball at the surface, which is where the trade name red snakehead comes from; adults lose it for a blue-black back and pale belly. Breathing air, it holds warm swamps, ponds and reservoirs across Southeast Asia where oxygen is scarce. Parents guarding a brood will charge anything that approaches, including animals many times their own size.
fishdesc.riverfishing.goliath_tigerfish: Thirty-two dagger teeth, each seating into a socket in the opposing jaw, close on prey in the rapids and deep runs of the Congo. The body is silver with faint dark lines along the flanks and blood-red fins, and the heaviest reach fifty kilograms. It hunts by sight in fast water, mostly at first and last light, and Congolese accounts of it taking small crocodiles are hard to disprove.
fishdesc.riverfishing.green_sunfish: Stockier than most sunfish and much bigger in the mouth, with turquoise squiggles across the cheeks, a black ear flap edged in pale, and orange piping along the fins. It survives water that would finish its relatives, hot and muddy and short of oxygen, so it turns up in stock ponds and creeks barely worth a name. Weight for weight it is among the pushiest fish in North America.
fishdesc.riverfishing.helicopter_catfish: Deep pools and undercut banks of Indian and Southeast Asian rivers hold this pale, elongated catfish through the day; it moves once the light has gone. The mouth opens back past the eyes, two long barbels stream from the upper jaw, and the anal fin runs almost the whole length of the belly. Voracious even by catfish standards, it swallows fish nearly half its own length.
fishdesc.riverfishing.himalayan_mahseer: Scales like burnished coins, thick rubbery lips and a deeply forked tail mark the golden mahseer of the Himalayan foothills. It holds in fast, boulder-strewn rivers, working pools and rapids for algae, insects, fruit dropped from the bank and any small fish within reach. Old records run well past a hundred kilograms, and it earned the name tiger of the river by turning the current to its own use.
fishdesc.riverfishing.iridescent_shark: The metallic sheen of the young gives the fish its name, though it fades to plain slate grey as the fish grows on towards forty kilograms. The skin carries no scales, the dorsal fin stands tall and shark-like, and the eyes sit low on the head. Shoals travel long distances up the Mekong, feeding near the bottom on plants, crustaceans and whatever small fish they overtake, without any real appetite for hunting.
fishdesc.riverfishing.kaluga_sterlet_hyb: A cross raised in hatcheries: the kaluga side brings bulk, a wide crescent mouth and an appetite for fish, the sterlet a narrow pointed snout, fringed barbels and the habit of maturing years earlier. Five rows of bony scutes stay in place, growth is quick, and the fish forages the cold beds of Amur-basin rivers for larvae, molluscs and small fish alike. Such vigour is usual in first-generation sturgeon crosses.
fishdesc.riverfishing.kaluga_sturgeon: Grey-green over a white belly, armoured in five rows of bony plates, the great sturgeon of the Amur reached a tonne in the old records. Unlike most of its family it is an outright predator, and chum salmon running upriver are its main food, taken with a wide crescent mouth built for the job. It can live past fifty years, and poaching for roe has pushed it to the edge.
fishdesc.riverfishing.kuria_labeo: The mouth is a downturned sucker with thick, fringed lips, made for rasping algae and soft debris off stones; small scales and a pored snout finish the picture. Rivers and reservoirs across northern India, Bangladesh and Myanmar hold it close to the bed, usually in loose company. It grows longer than most of its genus and can hold a place in heavy current for hours without visible effort.
fishdesc.riverfishing.kuria_labeo_catla_: Two carp shapes collide in one fish: the broad head and deep body of the catla, the thick fringed lips and blunt snout of the kuria labeo. Feeding follows the labeo side, along the beds of rivers and warm lowland lakes across monsoon Asia rather than at the surface. Size is the catla's gift, well past a metre. It pulls in long, dogged runs rather than sudden bursts.
fishdesc.riverfishing.laced_moray: Black polygons crowd a cream skin until the pattern looks like honeycomb held up to the light, and the same speckling runs on into the mouth. Reef ledges and coral rubble from East Africa to the East Indies hold it, one head showing, the body wedged out of sight. Night is its hour. A second set of jaws in the throat drags prey backward, so nothing swallowed comes out again.
fishdesc.riverfishing.lake_sturgeon: Five rows of bony scutes, a shovel snout, four barbels beneath it: a design that has needed no revision in a very long time. It works cold northern rivers and lake floors of North America, vacuuming larvae, snails and crayfish from the silt. Females spawn every four or five years, and single fish outlive the people who tag them. For all its bulk it leaps clear of the water.
fishdesc.riverfishing.lake_trout: Cream spots scattered over olive-green, a deeply forked tail and white piping along the lower fins mark a char rather than a true trout. Cold water rules it: deep basins through summer, shallow rocky shoals in autumn, where it spawns at night over clean cobble. Growth is slow enough that a forty-year-old fish raises no eyebrows. It resists in heavy short surges, then settles and leans on the bottom.
fishdesc.riverfishing.largemouth_smallmo: The cross shows first in the jaw: it ends right under the back of the eye, too far for a smallmouth, not far enough for a largemouth. Flanks carry both signatures at once, faint bronze bars crossing a broken dark stripe. It holds mid-water around rock and sunken timber in lakes and ponds of North America. Spring turns the males into nest-guarding bullies that charge anything that moves.
fishdesc.riverfishing.largemouth_yellowf: Brassy gold flanks, coarse scales and a mouth far wider than any carp needs, which hints at what changes with age. Young fish pick insects from gravel; adults in the Orange and Vaal hunt smaller yellowfish outright. It is the largest African yellowfish, over twenty kilos, and lives in that river system and nowhere else. Rocky rapids and the deep runs below them are its ground.
fishdesc.riverfishing.longnose_alligator: Enamelled diamond scales sheathe the whole body, and the beak reports the parentage: longer and narrower than an alligator gar's, thicker and blunter than a longnose's, with the second row of teeth showing only in patches. It hangs just under the surface of southern swamps and backwaters, log-still until something swims past. A swim bladder plumbed to the throat lets it breathe air where other fish suffocate.
fishdesc.riverfishing.longnose_gar: Nothing else in fresh water carries a snout like this: twice the length of the head, pencil-thin, set with a single row of needle teeth. Olive above, dark-spotted on fins and tail, the body sheathed in ganoid scales that turn a knife blade. It lies at the surface of warm swamps and backwaters, rising now and then to gulp air. Its roe is poisonous to anything that tries it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.longsnout_disticho: Six or seven dark bars fall across an orange-red body, and the snout runs out to a soft point above a small downturned mouth. A startled fish raises its dorsal like a flag. Rivers of the Congo basin and flooded forest margins suit it, and it grazes mid-water by day on soft plant growth. Under forty centimetres, it is a modest example of a large genus.
fishdesc.riverfishing.lute_fish: Deep, flat and silver as a coin, with a head too small for the body and a mouth smaller still. It needs no bigger one: the diet is mud, algae and drifting plant matter, sieved from mid-water in the Nile, the Niger and Lake Chad. Floods draw whole shoals onto the plains to spawn. Seven kilos is a heavy fish, and prized food from Egypt to Senegal.
fishdesc.riverfishing.lyretail_pleco: Charcoal armour, a scatter of white dots in young fish, and a tail drawn out into two long trailing points, which is where the name comes from. Every plate bristles with small backward-facing spines, so anyone handles one bare-handed exactly once. After dark it grazes sunken wood and stone on the beds of Amazon and Orinoco tributaries, reaching a full metre. Peaceable, except towards other plecos claiming the same log.
fishdesc.riverfishing.malayan_mahseer: Scales the size of coins, a bronze-gold flank and a thick rubbery lobe on the lower lip identify the fish Borneo calls empurau. It holds in cool hill rivers and deep pools under rapids, working the bottom at first and last light. Its standing rests on diet: fish fattened on fallen engkabang fruit take on the taste, and fetch more per kilo than anything else in Malaysia.
fishdesc.riverfishing.map_puffer: Dark lines radiate from the eye across a pale body, a pattern closer to a contour map than to stripes, and the belly is barred black on white. Four fused teeth make a beak that crunches sponges, coral and shellfish over Indo-Pacific reefs and lagoon flats. Threatened, it swallows water and swells into a taut ball. Flesh and organs carry tetrodotoxin, so the reef leaves it alone.
fishdesc.riverfishing.marbled_lungfish: Slate marbling over a body built like an eel, the paired fins reduced to soft threads that feel along the bottom. Lungs make air the main supply, and a fish held under water will drown. When the swamps of the Nile and Lake Victoria dry out, it burrows into mud and waits out the drought in a cocoon of hardened slime. Its genome is the largest of any animal.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mekong_giant_catfi: Adults lose both teeth and barbels, ending up with a broad flat head, small low-set eyes and a mouth made for scraping algae: three hundred kilos of catfish living on plants. It keeps to the main Mekong channel, wintering in deep pools and running upstream in the warm months to spawn. The heaviest confirmed fish weighed 293 kilograms. Numbers have fallen so far that every mature adult counts.
fishdesc.riverfishing.mozambique_tilapia: Olive-grey and forgettable most of the year, the male goes near-black to breed, with white lips and red-edged fins, and digs a saucer-shaped pit in the shallows. The female takes the eggs into her mouth and keeps them until the fry can feed; at any later alarm they swim straight back in. Ponds, weedy lake margins and brackish river mouths of southern Africa all serve.
fishdesc.riverfishing.muskellunge: Where a pike is light-marked on dark, the muskie reverses it: dark bars and blotches over a pale flank, sometimes fading to plain bronze. The tail lobes end in sharper points and the cheek is scaled only on its upper half. It hunts weed edges and drop-offs in northern lakes, keenest in autumn as the water cools. The attack is one accelerating rush, often finishing above the surface.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nile_bichir: A row of small separate finlets runs down the back in place of a dorsal, and the pectorals sit on fleshy stalks it walks with along the bottom. Enamelled rhomboid scales fit edge to edge like mail. Days pass in cover among Nile swamps and floodplain pools; after dark it hunts small fish and insects, surfacing to breathe. The larvae hatch with feathery external gills, like tadpoles.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nile_blue_tilapia_: The barred tail fin comes from the Nile side, though the bars blur and break, while the head takes on the metallic grey of the blue parent. Cold tolerance arrives from the same source: the hybrid keeps feeding at temperatures where a pure Nile fish stands still and starves. Nearly all the offspring are male, which is exactly why farms from the Levant to the Delta keep making the cross.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nile_mozambique_ti: Colour is the whole point of this cross: a fault in black pigment leaves the fish orange to pinkish-white, the belly pale as a peach, with a few stray dark flecks. Body shape and growth come from the Nile parent, salt tolerance from the Mozambique, so it thrives in ponds from Ecuador to Java to the Zambezi. Otherwise it is tilapia throughout: mid-water, plant-fed, forever spawning.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nile_perch: Silver with a blue sheen, a jutting lower jaw and a black eye ringed in yellow, and it is the eye that settles the matter. It cruises open water in the great African lakes and the Nile, eating everything smaller than itself, which is how hundreds of cichlid species vanished from Lake Victoria. Two hundred kilos is the ceiling. Big ones run flat along the surface.
fishdesc.riverfishing.nile_tilapia: Count the bars in the tail fin: six to nine of them, dark, running its full depth, and the matter is settled. This is the most farmed cichlid on the planet, at home in warm rivers, ponds and swamp edges across Africa and in every country it has been carried to since. The female broods eggs and fry in her mouth, going a week or more without food.
fishdesc.riverfishing.northern_pike: Rows of pale bean-shaped spots over dark green, a flattened duck-bill snout and a body that is all shoulder and tail, built for a single accelerating lunge out of cover. Weed edges, flooded timber and quiet lake bays hold it, and it keeps hunting under the ice. Spawning comes early, in meltwater over flooded grass, before most other fish have stirred. Appetite makes no exception for its own kind.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ocellaris_clownfis: Three white bars, each outlined in black, cross a body of soft orange barely the length of a finger. It keeps to shallow warm reefs of the Indo-Malayan region, never further than a dash from the anemone whose stings its coat of mucus shrugs off. Daylight goes on squabbling over that host and chasing off larger neighbours. Every one hatches male; the biggest turns female.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ocellate_river_sti: A flat grey-brown disc scattered with yellow-ringed eyespots, and behind it a whip of a tail carrying a serrated, venomous spine. Days pass buried in the sand of Amazon and Parana channels, lakes and flooded forest, only the eyes showing. From dusk it works the dark for shrimp, molluscs and small fish. Unlike its marine relatives it never enters salt water, and the female bears live young.
fishdesc.riverfishing.paddlefish: Nearly a third of the length is a flat, blade-like snout studded with electroreceptors that pick out clouds of zooplankton in muddy water. The body behind it is smooth and scaleless, and a big Mississippi fish passes two metres and ninety kilos. It cruises open river and reservoir water with its mouth agape, straining food through fine gill rakers. Spring floods send it upstream to spawn over gravel bars.
fishdesc.riverfishing.palette_surgeonfis: Royal blue flanks carry a black brushstroke shaped like a painter's palette, and the tail is a wedge of pure yellow. At its base folds a scalpel-sharp spine, flicked out sideways when a bigger fish crowds in. Warm reefs from East Africa to the Indo-Malayan islands hold it above the coral, picking plankton through the day. Alarmed, it wedges into a crevice and locks itself there.
fishdesc.riverfishing.payara: Two lower canines long enough to need sockets in the upper jaw give this silver, mackerel-shaped hunter its other name of vampire fish. It holds in broken water below rapids on the Amazon and Orinoco, striking upward at first and last light to impale smaller fish, piranhas among them. The attack is one hard burst that spends most of its strength in seconds.
fishdesc.riverfishing.polka_dot_squeaker: Ink-purple skin sown with round white spots, and no two fish wear the same arrangement of them. Rivers and flooded forest of the Congo basin hold it near the bottom among sunken wood, where the night goes on insect larvae, worms and plant scraps. Daylight passes in shadow. Disturbed, it creaks aloud as the pectoral spines grind in their sockets, which is how the family got its name.
fishdesc.riverfishing.pumpkinseed: Palm-sized, deep and round as the seed it takes its name from, with wavy blue-green lines across the cheek and a scarlet crescent on the tip of the black ear flap. Warm weedy ponds and lake margins across eastern North America suit it, and it hangs in the weed all day. Pharyngeal teeth crush snail shells other panfish cannot manage. Spring puts the males on saucer nests in the shallows.
fishdesc.riverfishing.red_drum: Copper-bronze along the back, with a black eyespot at the base of the tail and sometimes a scatter of them. It roots nose-down over sand and mud in surf, estuaries and shallow bays of the American Atlantic and Gulf coasts, taking crabs, shrimp and mullet hardest at dawn and dusk. Muscles drumming against the swim bladder carry that sound above water. Old bulls pass forty kilos and spawn in autumn.
fishdesc.riverfishing.red_finned_mahseer: Himalayan foothill rivers from the Ganges to the Brahmaputra hold a barbel with scales the size of a thumbnail, thick rubbery lips and fins washed red. It sits in rocky pools and heavy current under rapids, turning the bottom over for algae, larvae, molluscs and fallen fruit. Monsoon water sends it far upstream to spawn. A fish of a metre and a half leans on the current all its life.
fishdesc.riverfishing.redbreast_sunfish: The ear flap gives it away: a long black tab with no pale rim, drawn out further than in any other sunfish, above an orange-red breast. Creeks and pond edges along the Atlantic slope of North America are its ground, near undercut banks and fallen wood. Insects make up most of the diet, taken from surface and bottom alike. In spring the males nest side by side.
fishdesc.riverfishing.redear_green_sunfi: From the redear parent come the deep body and the throat mill that crushes snails; from the green sunfish, a mouth far too big for a panfish and the temper to match. The cross outgrows both, shrugs off warm, oxygen-poor water, and comes out almost entirely male, hence its place in so many farm ponds. It hunts in short rushes through the middle water, taking larvae, snails and fry.
fishdesc.riverfishing.redear_sunfish: Shellcracker, they call it in the American South, and it earns the name: flat pharyngeal teeth grind snails and small clams to pieces, shell and all. Males carry a bright red margin on an otherwise black ear flap, above an olive flank with a brassy sheen. It keeps deeper and further from the weed than its relatives, over gravel and firm sand. Spring gathers it into dense nesting colonies.
fishdesc.riverfishing.redtail_catfish: Sooty above, chalk-white along a broad band down the flank, and finished off with a tail and dorsal fin the colour of hot brick. After dark it works the bottom of Amazon and Orinoco channels and flooded forest, swallowing whatever fits: fish, crabs, fallen fruit, now and then a bird. Disturbed, it goes deep and sits there like a sack of sand. Brazilians call it pirarara.
fishdesc.riverfishing.reedfish: Long and snake-like, without pelvic fins at all, and carrying a row of small separate flags along the back where a dorsal fin should be. Hard enamelled scales armour the body, and a pair of true lungs lets it gulp air and live in the stagnant swamps of the Niger delta. Nights go to hunting worms and larvae by scent. Over wet ground it wriggles from pool to pool.
fishdesc.riverfishing.reticulate_knifefi: Shaped like a blade: humped back, next to no tail fin, and one ribbon of an anal fin along the whole underside, whose ripple drives it forward or backward without turning. Fine pale rings net the dark body, hence the name. Swamps and floodplain pools of West Africa are its ground: roots by day, hunting from dusk. In foul water it breathes air through a lung-like swim bladder.
fishdesc.riverfishing.ripon_barbel: Named for the falls at the outflow of Lake Victoria, where it once massed in uncounted numbers. This is a heavy-shouldered highland barbel, brassy-scaled, with two pairs of barbels and a blunt snout for shifting stones. It grinds along the bottom of rocky rivers and lake margins after snails, larvae and plant matter, busiest at first and last light. Spring runs carry it up into fast tributaries.
fishdesc.riverfishing.roach_rudd_hybrid: Everything sits halfway: the mouth neither straight like a roach's nor tilted like a rudd's, the dorsal fin between the two, the fins orange but never the lacquer red of a true rudd. Such crosses turn up wherever both parents spawn over the same flooded grass, in slow European rivers and lakes. They shoal and feed quietly near the bottom, often outgrowing both parents while leaving few young.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rock_bass: Red eyes in a brassy-olive head, rows of dark dots along the flank, and a mouth too big for a fish this size. Boulder-strewn river runs and rocky lake shores in eastern North America suit it, where crayfish and minnows are taken in short furious rushes. Within a minute it can darken or pale to match the stone behind it. Come spring the males fan out gravel nests.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rohu: An arched back, a pointed snout and a fringed lower lip built to scrape rather than to seize. Rivers of India, Bangladesh and Myanmar hold it near the bottom, where it lives on algae, soft growth and detritus rather than prey. Each large scale carries a red-brown centre, giving the flank a stitched look. Monsoon floods set off spawning on the drowned margins, and old fish pass two metres.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rohu_catla_hybrid: The head belongs to the catla, broad and blunt with a great upturned mouth, while the body behind keeps the rohu's slimmer lines and tidy scaling. That mix feeds it from both directions: plankton sifted in the upper water, silt grubbed over on the bottom. Rivers and pond fisheries of the Indian subcontinent hold it, and in its first years it outgrows either parent. Spawning comes with the warm rains.
fishdesc.riverfishing.rohu_kuria_labeo_h: Both parents are labeos, so the differences are quiet ones: thick fringed lips and a small sucker of a mouth from the kuria labeo, the deeper body and sharper snout from rohu. It scrapes algae off stones and sunken wood in the rivers of northern India and Bangladesh, working hardest at dawn and dusk. A metre and a dozen kilos is the ceiling, well short of pure rohu.
fishdesc.riverfishing.royal_featherback: A knife of a fish out of the Mekong: humped back, a dorsal fin no bigger than a feather, and a continuous anal fin running to the tail tip. What sets it apart is the pattern of irregular dark bars over the rear body, instead of the neat ringed spots its relatives wear. It stands in sunken timber by day and hunts fish and shrimp from dusk.
fishdesc.riverfishing.saddled_bichir: Dark saddles drop over the back beneath a row of separate finlets that stand up like small sails. The body is armoured in hard, glossy scales, and the lower jaw juts past the upper into a face made for grabbing. Swamps and slow creeks of West and Central Africa hold it on the bottom by day; after dark it tracks prey by scent. Paired lungs let it breathe air.
fishdesc.riverfishing.salt_creek_pupfish: Barely longer than a thumb, this stubby silver fish of Death Valley keeps the harshest address in North America. Its shallow creeks, warm pools and roadside puddles run saltier than the sea and heat past what most fish tolerate. Males turn steel-blue and quarrelsome over spring territories, sprinting at rivals in short flicks. Midge larvae in the sunlit shallows carry them through the bright hours.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sauger: Rows of black spots on the spiny dorsal, dark saddles across a brassy back and a tail with no white tip separate this fish from its walleye cousin. Big turbid rivers suit it best, and a mirrored layer in the eye turns muddy dusk into good hunting light. It works the bottom steadily through autumn and runs far upstream in spring to spawn over gravel.
fishdesc.riverfishing.saugeye: Cross a walleye with a sauger and the offspring takes the blotchy saddles and tolerance of murky water from one parent, the white-tipped tail and the bulk from the other. It outgrows both, which is why reservoirs across the continent are stocked with it. Bottom-oriented and unhurried, it feeds hardest at first and last light, and pushes into rivers as autumn cools the water.
fishdesc.riverfishing.semutundu: Four pairs of barbels sweep back from a broad flat head, and a long adipose fin runs most of the way to the tail. Lakes, sluggish channels and flooded swamp margins of tropical Africa hold it, always close to the bed. Night is its shift, spent hunting smaller fish over silt and drowned timber. Ugandan fishermen rate its flesh above almost anything else the Nile basin gives.
fishdesc.riverfishing.senegal_bichir: A row of separate flag-like finlets along the back and thick diamond scales of enamelled armour give this African oddity a look borrowed from the Devonian. Paired lungs let it rise and breathe air, so swamps and shrinking floodplain pools that suffocate other fish suit it well. Eyesight is poor; after dark it tracks prey along the bottom by scent, sculling on fleshy pectoral fins. Fry carry feathery external gills.
fishdesc.riverfishing.short_tailed_river: Heaviest of the South American freshwater rays: a disc as wide as a door and a tail cut noticeably short. Sand and silt in the big rivers of the Parana system hide it, since it settles in, flicks a shallow pit over itself and waits. Molluscs, crabs and slow fish go under the disc, while a serrated venomous spine at the tail base deals with anything that stands on it.
fishdesc.riverfishing.shovelnose_sturgeo: Flat as a spade at the nose, with four fringed barbels in a straight row and a long whip trailing from the upper tail lobe. The smallest of North America's sturgeons keeps to swift sandy channels of the Missouri and Mississippi, grubbing insect larvae out of the bed. Cool water suits it, and most of the feeding happens after dark. Rivermen call it hackleback and salt its roe as caviar.
fishdesc.riverfishing.silver_catfish: Scaleless, flat-sided and bright as a coin, with a long anal fin running back to the tail and four pairs of barbels around the mouth. It keeps near the bed of African rivers, backwaters and flooded swamp, coming alive at dusk and through the night. The diet is whatever offers: insects, small fish, windfall fruit in flood season. Unlike most catfish, it travels in loose companies rather than alone.
fishdesc.riverfishing.six_banded_distich: Young ones glow orange with six black bars down the flank; the bars fade with age and a big fish ends up dull olive and slab-sided. Congo basin rivers hold it in midwater over sunken wood, where a small blunt mouth strips leaves, roots and algae. It grazes without pause through the whole of daylight. Eighty centimetres of stubborn vegetarian yields its spot at the snag to nothing.
fishdesc.riverfishing.smallmouth_bass: Bronze flanks crossed by dark bars, a red eye and a jaw that stops short of it settle any argument with its wide-mouthed relatives. Cool rocky lakes and clear gravel rivers are home, and crayfish make up most of the diet. Spring warms it into a temper; males fan out nests on the shallows and guard them. Pound for pound, few freshwater fish pull harder.
fishdesc.riverfishing.smallmouth_spotted: Where smallmouth and spotted bass share a river the two occasionally cross, and the temper of the result earned it the name meanmouth. From one parent come bronze barring and a hard, jumping fight; from the other, rows of dark spots below the lateral line and a tooth patch on the tongue. It holds midwater near rock in lakes and slow reaches. Old accounts of it charging swimmers refuse to die.
fishdesc.riverfishing.sockeye_salmon: At sea it is plain blue-backed silver; on the spawning run the body turns scarlet, the head goes olive-green, and the male grows a humped back and a hooked jaw. Alone among Pacific salmon it needs a lake, where the young rear a year or more before dropping down to salt water. Krill and copepods build that famously red flesh. Autumn brings the survivors back to their own gravel.
fishdesc.riverfishing.splake: Brook trout and lake trout cross willingly: the offspring keeps the pale worm-track marbling of the first across its back and the depth tolerance and heft of the second, with a tail forked halfway between them. It grows faster than either parent and matures early, and unlike most hybrids it can breed. Cold northern lakes and their inlet rivers hold it, mostly in midwater, feeding hardest as autumn closes in.
fishdesc.riverfishing.spotted_bass: Dark blotches below the lateral line run back in neat rows, and a rough patch of teeth sits on the tongue: small marks, but they settle any argument with a smallmouth. Current and a little colour in the water suit it, on rock in reservoirs and at the tails of river pools. Smaller than its cousins and readier to school, it feeds in the low light at either end of the day.
fishdesc.riverfishing.spotted_gar: Armour-plated in interlocking enamel scales and spotted from snout to tail fin, it hangs motionless under the surface like a waterlogged stick until something small swims close. Warm swamps, backwaters and weedy ponds suit it, and a vascular swim bladder lets it gulp air where the oxygen gives out. The strike is one fast sideways slash of the toothed beak. Its eggs are poisonous to anything that eats them.
fishdesc.riverfishing.spotted_seatrout: No trout at all but a drum, and it carries its name in black spots scattered over the back, the dorsal and the tail. Two canine fangs in the upper jaw and a paper-thin mouth finish the identification. Grass flats and estuary bottoms along warm coasts hold it, hunting shrimp and small fish at dawn and dusk. In autumn the males croak on their swim bladders across the spawning shoals.
fishdesc.riverfishing.starry_puffer: Adults are chalk-pale and stippled with black over every inch, while the young wear yellow with bold dark stripes: the same fish, two lifetimes apart. It passes a metre in length, which makes it one of the heaviest puffers on any reef. A fused beak crushes urchins, molluscs and coral through the daylight hours. The organs carry tetrodotoxin, and a frightened fish swallows water until it is a rigid ball.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tambaqui: Deep, slab-sided and dark below the lateral line, with molar teeth built to crack seeds. When the Amazon spills into the forest it moves in among the trunks and feeds on fruit and nuts dropping through the surface. The young filter plankton with fine gill rakers instead. Forty kilos is the ceiling for this piranha relative that gave up meat and became the mainstay of Brazilian fish farming.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tapah_catfish: A mouth that splits the head back past the eyes, a deeply forked tail and a low anal fin running almost to it mark out this Southeast Asian giant. Deep river pools and drowned timber hold it by day; after dark it hunts fish, and at any hint of danger it drives straight for the bottom. Two metres and ninety-odd kilos are on record. Dams and netting have thinned it badly.
fishdesc.riverfishing.terek_barbel: Two pairs of barbels, thick rubbery lips and a low-slung mouth built for grubbing between stones. It belongs to the Terek and other Caspian-slope rivers of the northern Caucasus, working gravel runs and the tails of pools. Insect larvae, molluscs and whatever the current delivers make up the diet, taken at first and last light. Half a metre is a big one, and the roe is toxic.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tiger_muskie: Pike crossed with muskellunge gives a fish barred in bold dark stripes over gold, and the pattern is what names it. Hardiness and rounded fin lobes come from the pike side, the pointed tail tips and the long lean build from the muskie. Being sterile, it spends nothing on eggs and puts it all into growth. It waits midwater along a weed edge and hits in one flat burst.
fishdesc.riverfishing.tigerfish: Interlocking dagger teeth show even with the mouth shut, horizontal black stripes run the length of a silver flank, and the tail burns orange. The Zambezi and other big African rivers are its water, where packs hunt midwater at dawn and dusk. Most of the fight happens in the air, in flat runs broken by jumps clear of the surface. At Schroda Dam it was filmed taking swallows on the wing.
fishdesc.riverfishing.trahira: Cylindrical, blunt-headed and mottled the colour of wet bark, with canines too long to sit neatly inside the jaws. Still backwaters, swamps and slow tropical creeks of South America suit it, where it lies in the weed and lunges once, hard. Low oxygen is no obstacle: it gulps air and sits out a dry season in a shrinking pool. Parents guard the nest and drive off anything that comes near.
fishdesc.riverfishing.trout_cichlid: Long, slender and blue-silver, it looks far more like a small trout than a cichlid, and the jaw opens wider than seems reasonable. It hunts open water in the warm lakes of tropical Africa, cruising at mid-depth over sunlit shallows and drop-offs alike. Smaller cichlids are its living, run down in short violent bursts. After dark the hunting all but stops.
fishdesc.riverfishing.vistula_barbel: The gravel runs of the upper Vistula and San are this barbel's whole world, worked nose-down while four short barbels read the stones for larvae, snails and whatever the current rolls past. Stockier and shorter than the common barbel, it seldom passes forty-five centimetres. Feeding peaks at first and last light, and again through autumn. Its roe is poisonous to people.
fishdesc.riverfishing.vundu_catfish: Africa's largest catfish runs past a metre and a half and fifty kilos, with a long fleshy adipose fin down most of the back, the mark that separates it from the sharptooth catfishes. Accessory breathing organs let it gulp air and hold out in swamps and shrinking pools. It forages the bottom by night, taking anything organic. On the Zambezi it is regarded with a certain superstition.
fishdesc.riverfishing.walleye: The eye gives it away: milky and glassy, backed by a mirror that gathers what little light reaches the bottom, with a clean white tip on the lower lobe of the tail. Cold northern lakes and rivers suit it, and autumn is its season. It sits deep through the bright hours, then moves onto shallow flats at dusk. The pull is heavy and dogged rather than showy.
fishdesc.riverfishing.warmouth: Three or four dark streaks radiate back from a red eye across the cheek, the surest mark on a thickset, mottled brown panfish with a mouth far too big for its size. Weedy ponds, backwaters and swamp edges suit it, ideally with a stump or an undercut bank to sit against. It waits, then takes crayfish and small fish in one short rush. Warm spring days bring it into the shallows.
fishdesc.riverfishing.west_african_lungf: Eel-shaped and slate-brown, with paired fins reduced to threads it uses to feel its way along the bottom, this lungfish must reach the surface to breathe or it drowns. Swamps, floodplain pools and sluggish rivers are its ground, hunted mostly after dark for snails, frogs and small fish. When the water goes, it burrows into mud and waits out the dry months in a cocoon of hardened mucus.
fishdesc.riverfishing.white_bass: Silver, deep-chested and marked with several dark horizontal stripes, the lower ones broken and stepped out of line. Schools roam open water in rivers and reservoirs, working in packs that drive shad to the surface until the water boils. Spring sends them upriver in dense spawning runs, and autumn brings a second spell of hard feeding. For a fish rarely over three kilos, it pulls with absurd persistence.
fishdesc.riverfishing.white_crappie: Six spines in the dorsal fin and faint vertical bars, instead of the scattered speckling of the black crappie, settle the identification. Loose schools gather around sunken timber and brush in lakes and slow rivers, holding at mid-depth. Spring is its season: nesting colonies in the shallows and the year's heaviest feeding. The membrane at the corner of the mouth is thin as wet paper, hence the old name papermouth.
fishdesc.riverfishing.white_sturgeon: North America's largest freshwater fish has been recorded at six metres and over eight hundred kilograms in the Fraser and Columbia, though such animals are a century's slow work. Five rows of bony scutes armour the body, and four barbels sweep the gravel ahead of a toothless, tube-like mouth. It holds in deep river holes and feeds mostly in the dark, on anything from shrimp to salmon.
fishdesc.riverfishing.whitemargin_moray: Chocolate skin dusted with dense white spots, and an interior of the mouth so pale that it gave the fish its other name, the whitemouth moray. It lives wedged into coral crevices on Indo-Pacific reefs, head out, gaping steadily because that is how it pushes water over its gills. A second set of jaws in the throat drags prey inward. Hunting is a dusk and night business.
fishdesc.riverfishing.whitespotted_puffe: Round as a barrel and sculling along on comically small fins, it is grey-green, dusted with white spots, with pale rings around the pectoral base and a yellowish belly. Shallow lagoons, reef flats and seagrass in warm seas are its ground, where teeth fused into a beak crush snails, urchins and coral. Alarmed, it swallows water until it becomes a spiny ball. The flesh carries tetrodotoxin.
fishdesc.riverfishing.wiper: A cross between striped bass and white bass, and it looks the part: the deep humped body and the broken, offset stripes come from the white bass side, the bulk and shoulders from the striper. Sterile, fast-growing and more tolerant of warm reservoirs than either parent, it has been stocked across the American Midwest. Schools run down shad in open water, and twelve kilos of hybrid does not quit.
fishdesc.riverfishing.yellow_bass: Brassy gold along the flanks with six or seven hard black stripes, the lower ones clearly broken and shifted backwards, which is the detail that separates it from the white bass. Small by the standards of its family, it rarely passes a kilogram and a half, and keeps to schools in the rivers and reservoirs of the Mississippi basin. Feeding runs strongest at first and last light, and again in autumn.
fishdesc.riverfishing.yellow_perch: Six to eight dark bars, tapering as they run down golden flanks, and orange-red lower fins that deepen in colour before spawning. Schools work the bottom along sand and the edges of weed in northern lakes and slow rivers, and cold water barely slows them, with autumn the best of it. The female lays her eggs in a long gelatinous ribbon, folded like an accordion over weed and branches.
